title: Coherent Transduction And Dynamical Back-action Between Light And Millimeter Waves
authors: Andr\'e Garcia Primo, Jiawen Liu, Amit Vankayala, Gabriel J\"ulg, Aleksei Gaier, Yazan Lampert, Ileana-Cristina Benea-Chelmus
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electro-optic transduction can bypass the loss and noise of electronic frequency conversion at millimeter-wave frequencies by parametrically converting signals onto low-loss, low-noise optical carriers, with coupling rates that grow with frequency. Exploiting this growth, however, requires shrinking both the millimeter-wave and optical resonators while preserving their quality factors and spatial overlap, which has not yet been achieved. Here, we demonstrate a triply resonant transducer whose optical and millimeter-wave resonators have comparable dimensions and minimal mode volumes. Coupled lithium niobate Fabry-P\'erot cavities, with free spectral ranges above 650 GHz and quality factors up to [MATH], form a photonic molecule integrated with a quarter-wave gold resonator at 263 GHz. The device reaches a vacuum electro-optic coupling rate [MATH] kHz, six times larger than previous millimeter-wave transducers and sixty times larger than at microwave frequencies. The device optically detects room-temperature thermal millimeter-wave photons at effective occupancies below one, which also serve as a calibration tone for transduction efficiency. Coherent transduction reaches cooperativities approaching 0.3, corresponding to internal efficiencies around 67%, accompanied by electro-optic dynamical back-action that broadens or narrows the optical resonances. These results demonstrate the advantage and feasibility of the frequency scaling of electro-optic coupling, establishing an architecture for weak-signal sensing and quantum and classical networking.

motivation: Electro-optic transduction can avoid the loss and noise of electronic millimeter-wave frequency conversion, but achieving strong coupling requires shrinking resonators while maintaining high quality factors and spatial overlap.
method: The authors integrate coupled lithium niobate Fabry-Perot optical cavities with a quarter-wave gold millimeter-wave resonator at 263 GHz, forming a photonic molecule with minimal mode volumes and high quality factors.
result: The device achieves a vacuum electro-optic coupling rate of several kHz, detects room-temperature thermal millimeter-wave photons, reaches cooperativities approaching 0.3 and internal efficiencies around 67%, and exhibits electro-optic dynamical back-action.
conclusion: These results establish frequency scaling of electro-optic coupling as a viable architecture for weak-signal sensing and quantum/classical networking with millimeter waves.

title: R\'enyi-2 Entanglement Of Purification Of The Symmetric Werner State
authors: Shokoufe Faraji
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper determines exactly the R\'enyi-2 entanglement of purification of the normalized symmetric Werner state in every local dimension [MATH] _2(W_{+,d})=\log_2{d^2+3d+4}. We establish additivity for tensor power and, more generally, additivity for finite products of symmetric Werner states with different local dimensions. A canonical purification and its products achieve these values globally, even when arbitrary joint purifications with unrestricted finite dimensional auxiliary systems are allowed. We further examine perturbations away from the symmetric endpoint, and prove the continuity of the optimal value at this endpoint; moreover, we show a sharp square root order of variation in the optimal purity, while the canonical purification remains asymptotically optimal in the achieved entropy as this weight goes to zero.
tldr: The paper exactly computes the Rényi-2 entanglement of purification for symmetric Werner states in all local dimensions and proves additivity and continuity properties.
motivation: Entanglement of purification is a key entanglement measure, but exact values are known only in limited cases; symmetric Werner states provide a natural family for testing additivity and optimal purification behavior.
method: The authors derive an exact formula for the Rényi-2 entanglement of purification of the normalized symmetric Werner state and construct canonical purifications that achieve the optimum, including for tensor products with different local dimensions.
result: They obtain the formula log2(d^2+3d+4), prove additivity under tensor powers and finite products, establish continuity at the symmetric endpoint, and show a sharp square-root variation in optimal purity under perturbations.
conclusion: These results provide exact entanglement-of-purification values for an important symmetric family and clarify additivity and continuity properties relevant to entanglement theory.

The authors show that a canonical purification—essentially a specific isometry from the symmetric subspace to a larger space—achieves these values globally, even when arbitrary joint purifications with unrestricted finite-dimensional auxiliary systems are allowed. This establishes that the canonical purification is optimal for all such products. The paper further analyzes perturbations away from the symmetric endpoint: it proves continuity of the optimal value at the endpoint and shows a sharp square-root order of variation in the optimal purity as the perturbation weight goes to zero, while the canonical purification remains asymptotically optimal in the achieved entropy. The results provide a rare exact formula for a quantum information measure in arbitrary dimension and shed light on the structure of optimal purifications for highly symmetric states.

title: Early Fault-Tolerant Magic State Synthesis And Spacetime Efficient Analog Rotations With Color Code On A Superconducting Quantum Processor
authors: Sean Garner, Aaron Hoyt, Shuwen Kan, Samuel Stein, Chenxu Liu, Ang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With recent improvements to syndrome extraction scheduling and decoding, and the availability of complete transversal Clifford operations and lattice surgery, color code is an especially promising platform for quantum processors with local connectivity. The key ingredient for universal computation is thus generating useful magic states with limited resources. Space-Time Efficient Analog Rotations (STAR) and Fault-tolerant magic state synthesis (MSS) are two such methods for magic state generation, targeted for near-term and long-term quantum computing, respectively. In this work, we perform the first implementations of both magic state paradigms on a superconducting quantum processor. We present a STAR-type injection protocol on the color code, with favorable error rate and spacetime costs versus prior protocols on both the color and surface codes. We then implement a MSS factory by performing multi-patch magic state cultivations, interleaved with transversal Clifford operations, and lattice-surgery magic state teleportation. Under post-selection, we achieve a kickback tomography correct sign probability of [MATH] on cultivated [MATH] states, [MATH] tomographic fidelity on logical analog rotation states, and [MATH] fidelity on synthesized logical magic states consuming 3 cultivated [MATH] states, 3 transversal Hadamard operations, and real-time feed-forward [MATH] corrections during magic state teleportation. We compare the efficacy of post-selection, Most-Likely-Error (MLE) decoding, and concatenated-matching decoding throughout, highlighting the potential of end-to-end color code computation.
tldr: The paper reports the first implementations of STAR-type magic state injection and fault-tolerant magic state synthesis using color codes on a superconducting quantum processor.
motivation: Color codes are promising for local-connectivity quantum processors because they offer transversal Clifford operations and lattice surgery, but universal computation requires resource-efficient magic state generation.
method: The authors implement a STAR-type injection protocol and a multi-patch magic state cultivation factory interleaved with transversal Clifford operations and lattice-surgery magic state teleportation, comparing post-selection, most-likely-error decoding, and concatenated-matching decoding.
result: Under post-selection, they achieve a kickback tomography correct sign probability on cultivated states, tomographic fidelity on logical analog rotation states, and fidelity on synthesized logical magic states using cultivated states, transversal Hadamards, and real-time feed-forward corrections.
conclusion: The work highlights the potential of end-to-end color-code computation and demonstrates practical magic state paradigms on superconducting hardware.

title: Measurement-angle Control Of A Continuously Monitored Quantum Oscillator: Purification Limits And Optimal Protocols
authors: Ralph Sabbagh, Olga Movilla Miangolarra, Andrew N. Jordan, Tryphon T. Georgiou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the dynamic purification of a continuously monitored quantum harmonic oscillator coupled to a thermal bath, where the control is the quadrature measurement angle of up to two detectors with prescribed strengths and efficiencies. Within the Gaussian regime, the conditional state covariance obeys a deterministic Riccati equation, and we ask what purity can be reached and sustained by manipulating the angle in time, in analogy with rapid-purification protocols for qubits. We propose, analyze, and compare constant-rate, greedy, vibrational, and variational monitoring strategies on the basis of sustained purity starting from the thermal bath state, and quantify to what extent they are able to maintain higher purity levels compared to lab-fixed or phase-locked detectors. We highlight structural features, operational limits, and optimal protocols from each strategy and study how model parameters shape control performance. We observe that in the absence of measurement-frame anisotropy, the time-dependent strategies achieve higher but similar performance. Once this symmetry is broken, their performances diverge, either improving or worsening depending on the relative timescales of oscillator dynamics, thermalization, and measurement.
tldr: The paper analyzes measurement-angle control strategies for purifying a continuously monitored Gaussian quantum oscillator coupled to a thermal bath and identifies purification limits and optimal protocols.
motivation: Continuous measurement can purify quantum states, but for harmonic oscillators subject to thermal noise the achievable purity, operational limits, and optimal measurement-control strategies are not well understood; rapid-purification protocols for qubits motivate this extension.
method: Within the Gaussian regime, the conditional state covariance obeys a deterministic Riccati equation. The authors propose and compare constant-rate, greedy, vibrational, and variational monitoring strategies for the quadrature measurement angle of up to two detectors with prescribed strengths and efficiencies.
result: Time-dependent measurement-angle strategies can sustain higher purity than lab-fixed or phase-locked detectors. Without measurement-frame anisotropy, the strategies perform similarly; once the symmetry is broken, their performance diverges, improving or worsening depending on the relative timescales of oscillator dynamics, thermalization, and measurement.
conclusion: The study highlights structural features, operational limits, and optimal protocols for measurement-based purification of monitored oscillators, showing that measurement-frame symmetry and timescale separation are key determinants of control performance.

title: The Exact Information Cost Of Randomized Measurements In Quantum Metrology
authors: Jiaxin Liu Wanqing Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized measurements provide state-independent readout for multiparameter quantum sensing. Although 3-designs retain a constant fraction of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for every pure state, we show that 2-designs need not. In dimension \(d\), complete mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) retain exactly \(1/(d+1)\) of the QFI in the worst state and direction, attaining the universal lower bound for 2-designs built from orthonormal bases; symmetric informationally complete (SIC) measurements retain exactly \((1-1/)/d\). The loss comes from aligned blind spots. Relative to a basis, pure-state changes split into population and phase parts of equal dimension, but probabilities respond only to the former. Mutual unbiasedness turns a population change for one basis into a phase change for every other. The worst case already occurs for a qubit encoded in two levels. Independent random bases instead scatter their blind spots. In sufficiently large dimensions, five Haar-random bases retain, with high probability, a dimension-independent QFI fraction for every pure state and direction. Random Clifford measurements on any number of qubits retain exactly one third. Thus blind-spot geometry, not second-order symmetry alone, controls worst-case metrological performance.
tldr: The paper determines exact worst-case quantum Fisher information retained by randomized measurement designs, showing that blind-spot geometry controls metrological performance.
motivation: Randomized measurements offer state-independent readout for multiparameter quantum sensing, but the worst-case information loss for different measurement designs was not fully understood.
method: The authors analyze QFI retention for 2-designs built from orthonormal bases, mutually unbiased bases, SICs, Haar-random bases, and random Clifford measurements, using a geometric argument about aligned blind spots.
result: Complete MUBs retain exactly 1/(d+1) of the QFI in the worst case, SICs retain a dimension-dependent fraction, five Haar-random bases retain a dimension-independent fraction with high probability, and random Clifford measurements retain exactly one third.
conclusion: Worst-case metrological performance is governed by blind-spot geometry rather than second-order symmetry alone, clarifying the information cost of randomized measurements.

title: Zero Mode, Zero Influence: Spatial-derivative Coupling In Particle Detectors
authors: Eduardo Mart\'{i}n-Mart\'{i}nez, Ireneo James Membrere, Adam Teixid\'{o}-Bonfill
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is common in particle detector models in cavity QED to often omit zero modes or assume their state, compromising causality or introducing ambiguity in their predictions. We show that spatial-derivative coupling eliminates both problems. For free massless scalar fields in static periodic or Neumann cavities of any spatial dimension, cavity-frame spatial derivatives annihilate the zero-mode operator while preserving microcausality. Detector dynamics and entanglement harvesting then depend only on the reduced detector-oscillator state, nonperturbatively and even with initial correlations with the zero mode. Time derivatives and moving-detector rest-frame spatial derivatives can retain zero-mode state dependence not compromising causality. Realized through current coupling in superconducting circuits, spatial-derivative coupling thus makes zero-mode state assumptions unnecessary.
tldr: Spatial-derivative coupling in cavity-QED particle detectors eliminates zero-mode state dependence while preserving microcausality, making zero-mode assumptions unnecessary.
motivation: Particle detector models in cavity QED often omit zero modes or assume their state, which can compromise causality or introduce ambiguity in predictions.
method: The authors analyze free massless scalar fields in static periodic or Neumann cavities of arbitrary dimension and show that cavity-frame spatial-derivative coupling annihilates the zero-mode operator. They examine detector dynamics and entanglement harvesting nonperturbatively, including initial correlations with the zero mode.
result: Detector dynamics and entanglement harvesting depend only on the reduced detector-oscillator state under spatial-derivative coupling, while time derivatives and moving-detector rest-frame spatial derivatives may retain zero-mode dependence without breaking causality.
conclusion: Spatial-derivative coupling provides a consistent way to avoid zero-mode state assumptions in particle detector models and can be realized through current coupling in superconducting circuits.

title: Distance To Integrability And Complexity
authors: Sean Casey, Marius de Leeuw, Tristan Mcloughlin, Sergiy Zhuk
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider nearest-neighbour interactions on spin-1/2 chains. We find the full set of integrable models of this form and apply a numerical algorithm to determine the "closest" integrable model for a given Hamiltonian. This allows us to define a model-independent distance to integrability. We show that standard measures of chaos interpolate between integrable and chaotic values with increasing values of this distance. However, there is a large variation across models and the distance to integrability provides additional information not directly provided by these diagnostics.
tldr: The paper defines a model-independent distance to integrability for nearest-neighbour spin-1/2 chains and studies how standard chaos measures vary with this distance.
motivation: Integrability versus chaos in many-body spin chains is usually diagnosed by model-dependent measures; the authors aim for a quantitative, model-independent notion of how far a Hamiltonian is from integrability.
method: They enumerate integrable nearest-neighbour spin-1/2 chain models and apply a numerical algorithm to find the closest integrable model for a given Hamiltonian, defining a distance to integrability.
result: Standard chaos diagnostics interpolate between integrable and chaotic values as the distance to integrability increases, but the relation varies substantially across models and the distance provides extra information beyond these diagnostics.
conclusion: Distance to integrability is a useful complementary tool for characterizing quantum chaos and integrability in spin-chain systems.

The distance to integrability thus provides complementary information beyond traditional chaos indicators, offering a new tool for characterizing quantum dynamics.

title: Quantum Simulation Of Real-time Yukawa Dynamics With Qubits And Qumodes
authors: Jack Y. Araz, Jeffrey Forshaw, Ross Jenkinson
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time quantum simulation of field theories offers access to scattering and decay dynamics, circumventing the limitations of Euclidean lattice methods. However, representing bosonic fields on qubits requires a finite-dimensional approximation and can entail costly multi-qubit operations. Hybrid qubit-qumode architectures avoid this by encoding bosonic fields directly in oscillators. We formulate scattering in the (1+1)-dimensional Yukawa theory for such a device, with staggered fermions on qubits and the scalar on qumodes. Trapped ions are a natural candidate, with the fermions on the internal states of the ions and the scalar on their collective motion, so that the Yukawa coupling becomes a native spin-dependent displacement. Emulating the device with tensor networks, we study the decay of a single scalar particle and fermion-antifermion scattering around the resonance region, using observables that can be measured on the device natively. We compare the results with those obtained using lattice perturbation theory. The emulation is able to resolve corrections beyond the Dyson summation of the one-loop self-energy.
tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid qubit-qumode trapped-ion approach for real-time quantum simulation of (1+1)-dimensional Yukawa theory and emulates it with tensor networks.
motivation: Real-time quantum simulation of field theories can access scattering and decay dynamics beyond Euclidean lattice methods, but bosonic fields are costly to encode on qubits alone; hybrid qubit-qumode architectures can encode bosons directly in oscillators.
method: The authors formulate Yukawa scattering with staggered fermions on qubits and the scalar field on qumodes, using trapped ions as a natural platform where the Yukawa coupling becomes a native spin-dependent displacement, and they emulate the device with tensor networks.
result: The emulation studies single-scalar decay and fermion-antifermion scattering near resonance, compares with lattice perturbation theory, and resolves corrections beyond the Dyson summation of the one-loop self-energy.
conclusion: Hybrid qubit-qumode architectures, particularly trapped-ion implementations, are promising for real-time quantum simulation of field theories with native bosonic degrees of freedom.

title: Compressed Oracle Duality: A Simple Framework For Knowing What Quantum Adversaries Know

abstract: ArXiv:2611.00609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.

title: Discovering Models For Experimental Quantum Systems With Agentic Ai
authors: Hannah C. Kleidermacher, Bennet Windt, Miguel Bello, James Zou, Jelena Vu\v{c}kovi\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central obstacle in realizing color center cavity-QED-based quantum technologies is inhomogeneity, or disorder, among individual emitters. As the number of emitters increases, so does the complexity of the experimental data, making it difficult to quantify the present physical mechanisms of disorder. Here we introduce an artificial intelligence-driven model discovery framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent, equipped with tools and a structured workflow, proposes candidate Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models, generates computational tools, and quantitatively evaluates competing physical hypotheses. We apply the workflow to three previously published experimental cavity-QED datasets collected from color centers in diamond and silicon carbide. Across the experiments, the agent successfully identifies physical models for the system and characterizes the disorder. In assessing reproducibility, we find that run-to-run variability is concentrated primarily in the research plan generation step, while the computational analysis itself is substantially more consistent. Our results suggest that structured LLM agent workflows can support model discovery from quantum optical experimental data while simultaneously allowing for human expert supervision and collaboration.
tldr: An LLM-based agentic workflow automatically discovers Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models from experimental cavity-QED data of inhomogeneously broadened colour centres in diamond and SiC.
motivation: Inhomogeneous broadening among emitters is a central obstacle for colour-centre cavity-QED technologies, and as emitter number grows the experimental data become too complex for manual identification of the underlying disorder mechanisms.
method: A large-language-model agent equipped with tools and a structured workflow proposes candidate Hamiltonian/Lindbladian models, writes the corresponding computational analysis code, and quantitatively scores competing physical hypotheses against three previously published datasets.
result: The agent recovers physical models and characterizes disorder across all three experiments; run-to-run variability is concentrated in the research-plan generation stage while the numerical analysis step is largely reproducible.
conclusion: Structured LLM agent workflows can assist human-supervised model discovery from quantum optical experimental data, offering a route to automated characterization of disorder in colour-centre platforms.

title: Semi-classical Analysis Of Noise Squeezing In Kerr Microresonators
authors: Sara Persia, Lev Fandeev, Fuchuan Lei, Bastian Ruhnke, Alexander E. Ulanov, Vaishali Adya, Victor Torres-Company, Tobias Herr
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kerr microresonators are integrated nonlinear devices widely used to generate classical optical frequency combs and nonclassical states of light. In particular, they provide a promising platform for squeezed light sources, which are important elements of emerging quantum sensing, communication, and computing technologies. Designing such sources requires numerical tools that efficiently incorporate realistic device physics and noise processes. Here, we show that established semi-classical frameworks based on the Lugiato-Lefever equation and the Ikeda map, instrumental in the development of classical light sources, can also predict the quadrature-noise properties of squeezed light when vacuum fluctuations are properly included. We consider three canonical configurations producing two-mode quadrature squeezing, single-mode quadrature squeezing, and intensity difference squeezing. In each case, the semi-classical simulations produce quadrature variances and noise spectra in close agreement with the quantum theoretical predictions. These frameworks therefore provide practical tools for designing squeezed light sources, with the capability to incorporate additional noise mechanisms, nonlinear effects, and complex resonator arrangements. More fundamentally, our results show that key experimental signatures of squeezing can be modeled as phase-sensitive amplification of properly normalized vacuum fluctuations within stochastic semi-classical field equations. This observation helps distinguish squeezing properties accessible through semi-classical field evolution from those intrinsically requiring a full quantum description.
tldr: The paper shows that semiclassical Kerr microresonator models can reproduce quadrature-noise and squeezing spectra when vacuum fluctuations are correctly included.
motivation: Kerr microresonators are promising integrated sources of squeezed light, but designing them requires efficient numerical tools that capture realistic noise and device physics.
method: The authors use Lugiato-Lefever and Ikeda-map semiclassical frameworks with properly normalized vacuum fluctuations to model three canonical squeezing configurations.
result: The semiclassical simulations yield quadrature variances and noise spectra in close agreement with full quantum predictions for two-mode squeezing, single-mode squeezing, and intensity-difference squeezing.
conclusion: Semiclassical field equations provide practical design tools for squeezed-light sources and clarify which squeezing signatures can be modeled without a full quantum treatment.

title: Triple Descent In Quantum Linear Regression
authors: Gabriele Lo Monaco, Salvatore Lorenzo, Alessandro Ferraro, Mauro Paternostro, G. Massimo Palma, Luca Innocenti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum linear regression models, such as quantum extreme learning machines and quantum fidelity kernels, are trained on features that can only be estimated from finitely many measurement shots. Sampling noise is usually treated as a nuisance that more shots suppress; we show instead that it can fundamentally reshape the instabilities of the learning problem. As the number of measurement outcomes grows, the prediction error displays a triple-descent profile, with two peaks of fundamentally different origins. The first, classical, peak occurs when the measurement first becomes informationally complete, is a direct analogue of double descent in classical linear regression, and is caused by ill-conditioning of the measurement itself. This peak affects predictions only through their variance, and is thus suppressed by increasing the number of shots at inference. The second, quantum, peak occurs beyond informational completeness when the number of outcomes matches the number of training states: shot noise populates unphysical outcome combinations and the regression fits these pure-noise features with large weights, corrupting the learned model itself. More training or test shots cannot remove this quantum peak, which disappears only in the ideal limit of exact training features. Using random-matrix theory, we derive the shape of both peaks analytically, accounting also for ridge regularization. Our results show that treating quantum features as exactly known overestimates classical instabilities while missing genuinely quantum ones.
tldr: The paper analyzes sampling noise in quantum linear regression and identifies a triple-descent prediction-error profile with distinct classical and quantum instability peaks.
motivation: Quantum linear regression models are trained on features estimated from finite measurement shots, but sampling noise is usually treated only as a nuisance rather than as a factor that can reshape learning instabilities.
method: Using random-matrix theory, the authors derive the prediction-error curve as the number of measurement outcomes grows, including the effects of ridge regularization and shot noise at training and inference.
result: They find two peaks: a classical double-descent-like peak at informational completeness that affects variance and is suppressible with more shots, and a quantum peak beyond completeness when the number of outcomes matches the number of training states, which cannot be removed by more shots.
conclusion: Treating quantum features as exactly known overestimates classical instabilities while missing genuinely quantum ones, so sampling noise must be explicitly modeled in quantum linear regression.

title: A Block-encoding Approach To The Segawa-Suzuki Spectral Mapping Theorem
authors: Yohei Tanaka
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the Segawa--Suzuki spectral mapping theorem for abstract Szegedy-type quantum walks from a block-encoding viewpoint. Retaining both eigenspaces of the involution underlying the chiral symmetry yields a natural two-by-two block representation in which the usual discriminant operator and its counterpart form the diagonal blocks. The non-endpoint spectral mapping theorem then follows from an elementary Schur decomposition, substantially simplifying the original proof by avoiding its invariant-subspace decomposition and approximate-eigenvector arguments. The same framework establishes the result for the spectrum, point spectrum, and Fredholm essential spectrum and gives a direct block-theoretic description of the endpoint inherited and birth eigenspaces. We illustrate the construction with a one-dimensional split-step quantum walk.
tldr: The paper provides a simplified block-encoding proof of the Segawa-Suzuki spectral mapping theorem for abstract Szegedy-type quantum walks.
motivation: The original spectral mapping theorem for Szegedy quantum walks relies on invariant-subspace decompositions and approximate-eigenvector arguments, which are technically involved. The author aims to give a cleaner derivation using block-encoding and Schur decomposition.
method: The author retains both eigenspaces of the chiral symmetry involution to obtain a two-by-two block representation, with the discriminant operator and its counterpart on the diagonal. The spectral mapping theorem is then derived via elementary Schur decomposition, and the framework is applied to spectrum, point spectrum, and Fredholm essential spectrum.
result: The non-endpoint spectral mapping theorem follows directly from the block representation, avoiding the original invariant-subspace and approximate-eigenvector arguments. The construction also yields a block-theoretic description of endpoint inherited and birth eigenspaces, illustrated with a one-dimensional split-step quantum walk.
conclusion: Block-encoding gives a streamlined and unified proof of the Segawa-Suzuki spectral mapping theorem and clarifies the structure of endpoint eigenspaces for Szegedy-type quantum walks.

title: Maximal Input Entropy For Binary Two-deletion And Two-insertion Channels
authors: Wenlin Zhang Haobo Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2611.01064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under uniform transmission, we determine the received binary words that maximize input entropy for two-deletion and two-insertion channels. For two deletions the maximizers are exactly the two alternating words at every positive received length. For two insertions the same conclusion holds from received length five onward; we give all smaller cases and exact maximal values. The proof combines an embedding-count identity organized by runs with strict convexity estimates, and a grouping of two-position deletion masks. For every insertion radius we give the complete positive embedding histogram of an alternating received word. We also determine its three-deletion histogram for every length, and certify all three-deletion maximizers through received length twelve and all three-insertion maximizers through length eighteen by exact integer comparison. These computations give precise three-error conjectures with their small-length exceptions.
tldr: This paper determines binary received words that maximize input entropy for two-deletion and two-insertion channels, with extensions to three-error cases via computation.
motivation: Deletion and insertion channels are classical synchronization-error models where maximizing input entropy is relevant for capacity and coding analyses.
method: The authors use an embedding-count identity organized by runs, strict convexity estimates, and grouping of deletion masks; they also perform exact integer comparisons for three-deletion and three-insertion cases.
result: For two deletions, the maximizing received words are exactly the alternating words at every positive length; for two insertions the same holds from length five onward, with all smaller cases and exact maximal values given.
conclusion: The paper provides precise combinatorial characterizations and conjectures for binary deletion/insertion channels, but it is a classical coding-theoretic contribution without a quantum information or thermodynamic component.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks And Their Classical Surrogates On Long-range Strongly Correlated Models
authors: Tatiana A. Bespalova, R\'eka Schwengelbeck, Laura Mismetti, Johannes Schachenmayer, Ivano Tavernelli, Francesco Tacchino
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We benchmark quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) and their classical surrogates for phase differentiation in one-dimensional strongly correlated systems with beyond-nearest-neighbour terms. Using an anisotropic Heisenberg spin chain and an extended [MATH]-[MATH] Fermi-Hubbard model as representative spin and fermionic testbeds, we train QCNN classifiers on labelled ground-state datasets and map out finite-size phase diagrams. In hybrid setups, we employ Pauli backpropagation to express the QCNN measurement as a weighted sum of Pauli-string expectation values to be evaluated directly on input states, and study how truncation parameters control the trade-off between approximation accuracy and the size of the resulting Pauli expansion. Robust convergence is achieved for the Heisenberg model under aggressive truncation, whereas the Fermi-Hubbard model requires substantially looser thresholds, resulting in a sharp growth in retained Pauli strings and evaluation cost. Our results contribute to charting where hybrid quantum-classical training is viable for learning strongly correlated quantum states, and provide practical guidance for choosing truncation regimes in Pauli backpropagation-based surrogates.
tldr: The paper benchmarks quantum convolutional neural networks and classical surrogates for phase differentiation in long-range strongly correlated spin and fermionic models.
motivation: The authors aim to chart when hybrid quantum-classical training is viable for learning strongly correlated quantum states and to understand the cost of Pauli-backpropagation-based classical surrogates.
method: They train QCNN classifiers on labelled ground-state datasets for an anisotropic Heisenberg spin chain and an extended Fermi-Hubbard model, and use Pauli backpropagation with truncation to express QCNN measurements as weighted sums of Pauli-string expectation values.
result: Robust convergence is found for the Heisenberg model under aggressive truncation, while the Fermi-Hubbard model requires much looser thresholds, causing a sharp growth in retained Pauli strings and evaluation cost.
conclusion: The work provides practical guidance for choosing truncation regimes in Pauli-backpropagation surrogates and clarifies regimes where hybrid quantum-classical training is viable for strongly correlated quantum states.

title: Detector Placement Relaxes Efficiency Requirements For Detecting A Weak Coherent Link
authors: M. H. Yu, S. Y. Li, X. Z. Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A weak coherent link can produce unusually early arrivals without changing stationary count rates. Missed jumps along routes available without the link can produce similar records, obscuring its presence. On an eight-site ring, relocating the same detector losses exposes one more crossing on the easiest background route to hide, without changing the dynamics or leading link signal. At fixed error and a common observation-time scaling, the tolerated missed fraction and time-bin width follow fourth-root rather than square-root scaling with link strength. These requirements hold for every decision using the counting record and are met using three event counts per bin, with all elapsed time included. At the same stationary collected flux, where jumps are monitored can therefore determine the time resolution needed for weak-link sensing.
tldr: Detector placement can relax efficiency and time-resolution requirements for detecting a weak coherent link in a counting-record setting.
motivation: A weak coherent link can be obscured by background routes and missed jumps that produce similar counting records, making its detection difficult without optimized detector placement.
method: The authors analyze an eight-site ring model, relocate detector losses, and study how missed-fraction and time-bin-width requirements scale with link strength under a fixed error criterion.
result: They find fourth-root rather than square-root scaling for tolerated missed fraction and time-bin width, requiring only three event counts per bin while including all elapsed time.
conclusion: Where jumps are monitored determines the time resolution needed for weak-link sensing at a fixed stationary collected flux.

title: Curvature-Driven Density And Fluctuations In Interacting AOUPs Under Confinement
authors: Sandipan Dutta Renu Parashar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate interacting active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles (AOUPs) confined in harmonic and double-well potentials, combining mean-field theory, analytical approximations, and numerical simulations. We derive the stationary density, position and velocity correlations, correlation length, dynamical structure factor, and leading-order entropy production. Unlike established harmonic normal-mode descriptions, our framework incorporates steric interactions, persistent forcing, and spatially varying confinement curvature through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the many-body Hessian. Within a locally homogeneous approximation, the correlation length is controlled by persistence and local curvature, increasing as the effective restoring stiffness decreases and formally diverging at the instability of the linearized description. Entropy production, at leading nontrivial order in persistence, is governed by gradients of the effective curvature. Harmonic confinement provides a constant-curvature reference, whereas double-well confinement creates equilibrium-like regions near the minima and strongly nonequilibrium regions near the barrier. The barrier exhibits enhanced velocity and density fluctuations, soft collective modes, long-lived correlations, and increased entropy production. Persistence amplifies these effects, while steric crowding suppresses collective fluctuations. The dynamical structure factor reveals enhanced low-frequency contributions from soft modes. Our results establish how confinement geometry, active persistence, and interactions jointly regulate collective fluctuations and irreversibility in active matter.
tldr: A mean-field plus numerical study of interacting active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles in harmonic and double-well traps, deriving stationary densities, correlations, dynamical structure factor and leading-order entropy production controlled by confinement curvature.
motivation: Existing normal-mode treatments of confined active particles ignore steric interactions, persistent forcing and spatially varying curvature, so a framework is needed that captures how confinement geometry and activity jointly shape collective fluctuations and irreversibility.
method: Combines mean-field theory, analytical approximations and simulations, using eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the many-body Hessian within a locally homogeneous approximation to obtain correlation lengths, structure factors and entropy production to leading order in persistence.
result: Correlation length grows as effective restoring stiffness decreases and diverges at the instability of the linearized description; double-well confinement produces near-equilibrium regions at the minima and strongly nonequilibrium, high-fluctuation, long-correlation regions at the barrier, with persistence amplifying and crowding suppressing these effects.
conclusion: Confinement curvature, active persistence and interactions jointly regulate collective fluctuations and entropy production in active matter, extending beyond standard harmonic normal-mode descriptions.

title: A Counterexample To The Gyarmati-Matolcsi-Ruzsa Conjecture
authors: Chandra Nair, Aref Namayandeh, Zhaobang Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a counterexample to the non-abelian Gyarmati-Matolcsi-Ruzsa conjecture. The construction comes from an equivalent maximal-coupling entropy inequality, for which a counterexample can be found in a lower-dimensional group. We give an explicit cardinality counterexample in [MATH], the fourteenth direct power of the dihedral group of order [MATH].
tldr: The paper constructs a counterexample to the non-abelian Gyarmati-Matolcsi-Ruzsa conjecture using an equivalent maximal-coupling entropy inequality.
motivation: The conjecture concerns entropy inequalities in non-abelian group settings, and the authors aim to disprove it by finding a lower-dimensional group counterexample.
method: They translate the conjecture into an equivalent maximal-coupling entropy inequality and then provide an explicit cardinality counterexample in a direct power of the dihedral group.
result: The construction yields a counterexample in the fourteenth direct power of the dihedral group of order eight, disproving the conjecture.
conclusion: This is a classical information-theoretic/group-theoretic result with no direct quantum information or quantum thermodynamic content.

title: Clarkson--McCarthy Type Inequalities, Part Ii: Refinements, Unitary Orbits, Unitarily Invariant Norms And $\ell_s$--$\ell_s$ Estimates
authors: Teng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In previous work , the author established Clarkson--McCarthy type inequalities for several classes of operator families, including [MATH]--[MATH] estimates and mixed [MATH]--[MATH] estimates, by means of operator square-sum identities. The present paper has two main aims. First, using the tracial joint spectral measures recently introduced by O.~Hein\"avaara , we obtain several refinements of the McCarthy--Clarkson inequalities, one of which confirms a conjecture of Audenaert . Second, combining tools from matrix analysis with complex interpolation theory, we establish Clarkson--McCarthy type inequalities for unitary orbits, unitarily invariant norms, and [MATH]--[MATH] estimates, again in the framework of operator square-sum identities.
tldr: This paper proves refinements of Clarkson–McCarthy type inequalities for unitarily invariant norms and unitary orbits using tracial joint spectral measures and complex interpolation.
motivation: Clarkson–McCarthy inequalities bound Schatten p-norm differences of operator sums, and refinements have been conjectured (Audenaert); the author aims to prove such refinements and extend the framework to unitary orbits and unitarily invariant norms.
method: The author combines tracial joint spectral measures due to Heinävaara with matrix analysis tools and complex interpolation theory, working within the operator square-sum identity framework.
result: Several refinements of McCarthy–Clarkson inequalities are obtained, one confirming a conjecture of Audenaert, along with new Clarkson–McCarthy type inequalities for unitary orbits, unitarily invariant norms, and ℓ_s–ℓ_s estimates.
conclusion: The results sharpen a classical family of norm inequalities and extend them to broader operator settings, though the work is purely mathematical with no direct quantum-information application developed.

title: Mutual Information Estimation Via Triangular Transport Maps: Finite Sample Guarantees And Sample Allocation
authors: Fengyi Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite sample guarantees for transport based mutual information estimation. Mutual information can be estimated by first learning the conditional and marginal densities and then evaluating their log-density ratio by Monte Carlo. Given training samples, we use triangular transport maps to learn these densities and then compute the mutual information estimate on an independent batch of evaluation samples. For conditional density estimation using triangular transport maps, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees over realizable H\"older classes by viewing the conditional density as an ordinary density with respect to the product of the law of the conditioning variable and Lebesgue measure. This allows standard density estimation techniques to be applied directly to the conditional density estimation. These results yield finite sample guarantees for the resulting mutual information estimator and characterize how a fixed sample budget should be allocated between training and evaluation in order to minimize the mean squared error. Numerical experiments support the predicted training and evaluation error rates and illustrate the resulting sample allocation tradeoff.
tldr: The paper develops finite-sample guarantees for mutual information estimation using triangular transport maps and derives an optimal training/evaluation sample allocation.
motivation: Mutual information estimation typically requires learning conditional and marginal densities, and practical performance depends on how limited samples are split between training and evaluation.
method: The authors use triangular transport maps to estimate conditional and marginal densities, establish non-asymptotic guarantees over Hölder classes, and analyze mean squared error to optimize sample allocation.
result: They obtain finite-sample error guarantees for the mutual information estimator and characterize the training/evaluation sample budget tradeoff, supported by numerical experiments.
conclusion: The work provides a statistically rigorous framework for transport-based mutual information estimation, but it is a classical statistics contribution without quantum information or thermodynamic content.

title: Applying Changes To Ldpc Codes By Using 3-Induced Matchings And Eigenvalues
authors: Alireza Eshraghi Dehaghani, Sara Saeedi Madani, Dariush Kiani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The 2-switch operation for reducing the number of short cycles in Tanner graphs of LDPC codes has been utilized in some works. If this operation is appropriately applied to a 2-induced matching in a bipartite graph, then it surely preserves the bipartiteness of the graph. With a 2-induced matching, we have only one choice for applying this type of change to the graph. Using 3-induced matchings creates more potential and flexibility to apply certain changes to the Tanner graph. We present a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a 3-induced matching in bipartite graphs with girth at least 6. A 3-induced matching helps us to have more choices for applying a change to a bipartite graph while surely preserving the bipartiteness of the graph and keeping the degree sequences unchanged. Among all changes that we consider, we select the best change for reducing the number of cycles of length 6. The eigenvalues of subgraphs are used to reach a 3-induced matching, and a condition in some steps can be checked to ensure that the subgraph has at least one 3-induced matching. We present some numerical results regarding the steps at which the condition that guarantees the existence of a 3-induced matching is checked.
tldr: The authors generalize the 2-switch operation on Tanner graphs of LDPC codes to 3-induced matchings, giving a necessary and sufficient condition for their existence and using subgraph eigenvalues to select cycle-reducing modifications.
motivation: Short cycles in Tanner graphs degrade LDPC decoding performance, and the existing 2-switch operation offers only a single choice when applied to a 2-induced matching, limiting flexibility in graph modification.
method: Graph-theoretic analysis of bipartite graphs with girth at least 6 characterizes when a 3-induced matching exists, with subgraph eigenvalue conditions used to certify existence and to choose among candidate changes that preserve bipartiteness and degree sequences.
result: A necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of 3-induced matchings is established, enabling more flexible degree-preserving graph modifications, and numerical results illustrate checking steps for the existence condition and selection of changes minimizing 6-cycles.
conclusion: 3-induced matchings provide a richer toolkit than 2-switches for reducing short cycles in LDPC Tanner graphs, though the work remains within classical coding theory without a quantum error-correction treatment.

title: Optimal Estimation In Weak Value Amplification With A Position Pointer
authors: Jing-Hui Huang, Jing Zhang, Jian Ge, Lichao Liu, Wang Luo, Xiang-Yun Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally evaluate five estimators for weak-value amplification (WVA) using a position pointer to measure birefringence time delays. Two general approaches are considered: measuring the position shift [MATH] and measuring the probability change [MATH] of successful postselection. Specifically, five estimators are investigated: CCD-detected fringe shift [MATH], quadrant photodiode (PDQ) transversal voltage difference (XDIFF), and lock-in amplifier output phase [MATH] (for [MATH] measurement), as well as PDQ total output voltage (SUM) and CCD-detected average photon number [MATH] (for [MATH] measurement). The measurement precision is characterized by the Allan deviation over a range of input laser powers [MATH]. Generally, measuring the position shift [MATH] yields higher precision than measuring the probability change [MATH]. At [MATH]~mW, corresponding to a laser-power-limited regime, direct measurement of the fringe displacement with the CCD achieves a minimum Allan deviation of [MATH]~as, approaching the corresponding photon-statistical Cram\'er--Rao bound (CRB). At [MATH]~mW, corresponding to a detector-limited regime, PDQ detection combined with lock-in demodulation provides the best precision, reaching [MATH]~as and remaining close to the corresponding CRB. These results demonstrate that the optimal readout depends on the available optical power, detector dynamic range, and technical noise, providing practical guidance for selecting readout strategies in high-precision WVA-based metrology.
tldr: The paper experimentally compares five readout estimators for weak-value amplification in a birefringence time-delay measurement using a position pointer.
motivation: Weak-value amplification is used to enhance precision in quantum metrology, but the best readout strategy depends on optical power, detector dynamic range, and technical noise.
method: Five estimators are evaluated: CCD fringe shift, quadrant photodiode XDIFF, lock-in phase, PDQ SUM voltage, and CCD average photon number. Precision is characterized by Allan deviation versus laser power and compared with Cramér–Rao bounds.
result: At higher optical power, CCD fringe displacement reaches about the photon-statistical CRB; at lower power, PDQ detection with lock-in demodulation gives the best precision and remains close to its CRB.
conclusion: Optimal WVA readout depends on available optical power and detection regime, providing practical guidance for high-precision WVA-based metrology.

title: Equal Hamming Weights At Fixed Root Order And Applications To Constacyclic Mds Codes
authors: Hongfeng Wu Li Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a fixed positive integer [MATH], we study the prime powers [MATH] coprime to [MATH] for which all monic irreducible factors of [MATH] over [MATH] have the same coefficient Hamming weight. Cyclotomic orbit coefficients give a finite, effective classification of these fields. Outside finitely many computable characteristics, every factor has the support of its characteristic-zero orbit polynomial; the uniform condition [MATH] suffices. In each remaining characteristic, extension exponents reduce to divisors of [MATH], and an integer variance identity expressed by polynomial gcd degrees decides equal weight. The same coefficient data determine the full weight distribution. As an application, we prove that an MDS constacyclic code with an irreducible generator forces every irreducible polynomial of the same root order to have full support, including factors associated with different constacyclic constants. We develop its short-multiplier extension, give a prime-order cubic family, and establish an explicit quadratic-residue exclusion without a prime-square alphabet or a near-square length hypothesis.
tldr: The paper studies equal Hamming weights of irreducible factors of x^M-1 over finite fields and applies the results to constrain MDS constacyclic codes.
motivation: To understand the weight distribution of irreducible factors of cyclotomic polynomials and derive structural limitations on MDS constacyclic codes.
method: Uses cyclotomic orbit coefficients for classification, a variance identity involving polynomial gcd degrees to decide equal weight, and analyzes MDS constacyclic codes with irreducible generators.
result: Proves that an MDS constacyclic code with irreducible generator forces every irreducible polynomial of the same root order to have full support, yielding a uniform gcd and norm obstruction, and develops extensions with explicit exclusions.
conclusion: Provides new combinatorial constraints on classical constacyclic MDS codes and their irreducible factors, with potential implications for classical coding theory.

title: Application A Quantum Machine Learning Algorithm To The Applied Problem Of Modeling The Thermal Regime Of A Servers
authors: M. A. Remnev P. V. Buzin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing is a rapidly developed field of science. In the NISC era, quantum machine learning stands out, potentially outperforming classical machine learning. In this paper, we explore the applicability of quantum machine learning to a real-world application. We solved the problem of prediction of the temperature of GPUs in a high-performance computing cluster. We trained a quantum circuit to predict the temperature of each of the eight GPU of each cluster node based on 16 physical parameters. We demonstrated that quantum machine learning performs on this task just as well as classical machine learning. Furthermore, using model problems, we demonstrated that quantum machine learning can potentially outperform classical machine learning.
tldr: The paper applies a quantum machine learning circuit to predict GPU temperatures in a high-performance computing cluster, finding performance comparable to classical ML.
motivation: Quantum machine learning is rapidly developing and may outperform classical ML, so the authors test its applicability on a practical thermal-monitoring problem for servers.
method: They train a quantum circuit to predict the temperature of eight GPUs per cluster node from 16 physical parameters and compare it with classical machine learning baselines.
result: Quantum ML matches classical ML on the real GPU-temperature prediction task, and model problems suggest potential quantum advantage.
conclusion: Quantum machine learning is a viable approach for applied thermal-regime modeling, though the study provides no clear information-theoretic or thermodynamic advance.

title: Side-Channel Attack Prevention For Post Quantum Cryptography Algorithms: A 3D-Shield Approach
authors: Carl Benda, Eren Kurshan, Aydin Aysu, Paul Franzon
abstract: ArXiv:2611.01144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite their theoretical quantum attack resistance, practical implementations of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms remain susceptible to side-channel attacks. This includes all standard algorithms selected the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) such as Kyber/ML-KEM, Dilithium/ML-DSA, Falcon/FN-DSA and SPHINCS+/SLH-DSA. This paper proposes an alternative defense for side-channel resilience based on 3D integration that uses 3D hardware to shield the underlying cryptographic activity by introducing decoy keys and physical shielding through stacking. The proposed approach can complement other security measures (such as masking and shuffling) on protecting Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) that move computation to dedicated NTT chips. We outline the construction of our approach and validate the effectiveness on a generic attack targeting intermediate computation inside an NTT butterfly.
tldr: The paper proposes a 3D-integration-based hardware shielding scheme with decoy keys to protect NIST post-quantum cryptographic implementations (Kyber, Dilithium, Falcon, SPHINCS+) against side-channel attacks on the Number Theoretic Transform.
motivation: Post-quantum algorithms are mathematically resistant to quantum attacks but their physical implementations leak information through side channels, so hardware-level countermeasures are needed to complement masking and shuffling.
method: The authors outline a defense architecture that stacks dedicated NTT accelerator chips with physical shielding layers and injects decoy keys to obfuscate intermediate computations, then validate it against a generic side-channel attack targeting an NTT butterfly.
result: A construction is described and evaluated against a generic intermediate-value attack on the NTT butterfly, with the claim that 3D shielding plus decoys reduces leakage.
conclusion: 3D integration may offer a complementary physical layer of side-channel resilience for PQC hardware, though the work is an outline-level validation rather than a full security analysis.
