title: Leaving Quantum Bias On The Table: Pushforwards As A Path To Quantum Advantage In Constrained Optimization
authors: Chinonso Onah, Stuart Hadfield, Kristel Michielsen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constrained quantum samplers often produce infeasible outputs that retain information about good feasible solutions. We develop a post-measurement framework that constructs problem-dependent classical feasibility maps from constraint-violation statistics and pushes the raw quantum sampling law forward onto the feasible set. The probability of each repaired solution is the total raw mass of its repair preimage, enlarging the successful sampling event from a target feasible set to its full repair preimage. We derive exact identities for repaired success and expected cost, and separate repair-basin geometry from sampler-dependent probability concentration. For noisy implementations, we distinguish leakage from the encoded subspace from concentration loss within it. For permutation constraints, Hungarian maximum-overlap repair provides an O(n^3) implementation, which we study on traveling-salesman problems (TSP). We derive conditional repaired-success bounds and quantify how basin aggregation reduces the absolute-transfer budget required by these bounds. Noiseless simulations show that optimal repair basins contain selectively overweighted infeasible contributors. For an n=10 TSP instance, pushforward repair recovered the optimum using approximately 10^3 shots, compared with 10^6 shots in the original CE-QAOA workflow without repair. On a 127-qubit IBM processor, using encodings of up to 100 qubits, repaired candidates match reference tours on smaller benchmarks and improve them on larger instances. These results establish concentration of quantum probability on useful repair preimages as a design principle for constrained quantum optimization.
tldr: A post-measurement framework that pushes the raw output distribution of a constrained quantum sampler forward onto the feasible set via problem-dependent classical repair maps, substantially improving sampling success for constrained optimization such as TSP.
motivation: Constrained quantum samplers (e.g., QAOA with constraint encodings) often return infeasible bitstrings, yet those infeasible samples still carry information about good feasible solutions; this information is typically discarded.
method: Constructs feasibility/repair maps from constraint-violation statistics (Hungarian maximum-overlap repair with O(n^3) cost for permutation constraints), defines repaired success probability as the total raw probability mass of a solution's repair preimage, and derives exact identities and bounds for repaired success and expected cost, separating repair-basin geometry from sampler concentration and leakage versus concentration loss in noisy devices.
result: For an n=10 TSP instance, pushforward repair recovered the optimum with ~10^3 shots versus ~10^6 in the original CE-QAOA workflow; on a 127-qubit IBM processor with encodings up to 100 qubits, repaired candidates matched reference tours on small benchmarks and improved them on larger ones.
conclusion: Concentration of quantum probability on useful repair preimages is proposed as a design principle for constrained quantum optimization, offering large shot-budget savings and hardware-viable performance.

title: Exhaustive Construction Of Generalized Parent Hamiltonians For Matrix Product States
authors: He-Ran Wang, Lorenzo Gotta, Sanjay Moudgalya
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Characterizing local Hamiltonians that host interesting many-body states as eigenstates has been an important problem in quantum many-body physics. For matrix product states (MPS), there is a well-known construction of parent Hamiltonians that have the MPS as the frustration-free ground state. However, recent results on quantum many-body scars have shown that such a construction does not exhaust all possible Hamiltonians that have the MPS as an eigenstate. In this work, we develop an exhaustive construction of generalized parent Hamiltonians that have a given translation-invariant MPS as an eigenstate. These go beyond the conventional projector-based construction of frustration-free parent Hamiltonians, where each local Hermitian term has the MPS as an eigenstate, by allowing non-Hermitian telescoping terms that cancel out with periodic boundary conditions (PBC). We derive a local tensor equation that establishes a correspondence between inequivalent classes of generalized parent Hamiltonians, i.e., those that cannot be related using linear combinations with frustration-free Hamiltonians, and the MPS transfer matrix spectrum. We illustrate the connection to intrinsic physical properties, including non-Abelian symmetries and zero correlation length, and further extend this construction to block-injective MPS. Our framework hence provides a systematic bridge between generalized parent Hamiltonians and the local structure of quantum states.
tldr: The paper constructs generalized parent Hamiltonians that have a given translation-invariant matrix product state as an eigenstate, going beyond conventional frustration-free constructions.
motivation: Characterizing local Hamiltonians that host interesting many-body states is a central problem in quantum many-body physics, and recent quantum many-body scar results show that standard frustration-free parent Hamiltonian constructions are incomplete.
method: The authors allow non-Hermitian telescoping terms that cancel under periodic boundary conditions and derive a local tensor equation relating inequivalent classes of generalized parent Hamiltonians to the MPS transfer matrix spectrum, extending the construction to block-injective MPS.
result: They establish a correspondence between generalized parent Hamiltonians and MPS transfer matrix spectra, and illustrate connections to non-Abelian symmetries and zero correlation length.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic bridge between generalized parent Hamiltonians and the local structure of quantum states, but it is a quantum many-body/tensor-network contribution rather than a match to the specified research directions.

title: Quantum Algorithm For Weakly Correlated Molecular Electronic Ground States With Sub-quintic Scaling In The System Size
authors: Oskar Leimkuhler, Marvin Kronenberger, Davide Castaldo, Timothy Stroschein, Srushti Patil, Rebecca Tomann, Arta Safari, Marek Miller, Gemma C. Solomon, Matthias Christandl, Markus Reiher
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weakly correlated electronic structures are predominant among molecules, and are routinely solved with heuristic classical methods such as the ``gold standard'' CCSD(T) coupled cluster model, incurring a formal time complexity [MATH] in the number of molecular orbitals and with no guarantee of energy error [MATH] at or below chemical accuracy. In this work, a quantum algorithm is presented for ground state energy estimation of weakly correlated molecules using Trotterized time evolution, with an end-to-end quantum operations cost that scales as [MATH] in the limit of high-order product formulae when run as a low-depth, shot-noise limited algorithm, or [MATH] when scaling the simulation time [MATH]. The algorithm combines adiabatic state preparation using a smoothed Gevrey schedule with eigenstate filtering via quantum prolate diagonalization (QPD). Both steps of the algorithm rely on a size-independent spectral gap assumption, which is validated by numerical studies on alanine chains with up to 64 monomers. We benchmark the performance of our eigenstate filtering algorithm on a set of 28 molecules to compare our approach against prior phase estimation algorithms, finding that QPD achieves state-of-the-art cost tradeoffs for [MATH]-accurate results. Physical quantum resource estimates are obtained for running Trotter step circuits with up to 40 spin-orbitals, providing a clear path for scaling up quantum simulation of chemistry on early fault-tolerant hardware.
tldr: The paper presents a Trotterized quantum algorithm with adiabatic preparation and quantum prolate diagonalization for estimating ground-state energies of weakly correlated molecules with sub-quintic scaling.
motivation: Weakly correlated molecular electronic structure is central to chemistry but classical CCSD(T) has high polynomial cost and no guaranteed chemical-accuracy error bound, motivating quantum algorithms with better scaling.
method: The approach combines adiabatic state preparation using a smoothed Gevrey schedule with eigenstate filtering via quantum prolate diagonalization, assuming a size-independent spectral gap validated on alanine chains.
result: The end-to-end quantum operation cost scales sub-quintically, and benchmarks on 28 molecules show state-of-the-art cost tradeoffs for chemical accuracy, with resource estimates for up to 40 spin-orbitals.
conclusion: The algorithm provides a promising route to early fault-tolerant quantum simulation of chemistry, but it falls outside the researcher's focused areas of quantum information theory, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Finesse Evolution In A Bichromatic Cavity Under Blue And Red Resonant Illumination In Vacuum
authors: M. S. Caracas Nu\~nez, A. Kadakkavattathu, G. Gatta, L. Duca, N. Mizukami, C. Sias
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The long-term performance of high-finesse optical cavities depends on the stability of their mirror coatings under vacuum and under continuous exposure to high circulating power. In cavities supporting multiple wavelengths, a central question is whether degradation at one wavelength compromises performance at another. Understanding this interplay is essential for those cavity quantum electrodynamics experiments that need diverse optical fields for cavity stabilization, trapping, and light--matter coupling. Here, we investigate wavelength-dependent degradation and recovery of a bichromatic cavity with high-reflectivity coating at 455 nm and 671 nm in vacuum. Cavity ring-down measurements reveal a decrease in the 455 nm finesse from 7.7*10^3 to 1.9*10^3 after 11 hours of continuous exposure to high circulating power. Simultaneous measurements show no measurable degradation at 671 nm. Continuous operation at 671 nm, instead, produces no measurable degradation at either wavelength under the tested conditions. Comparison of oxygen depletion and Avrami-type loss models indicates kinetics compatible with nucleation and growth, without uniquely identifying the microscopic mechanism. We demonstrate partial recovery of the finesse with illumination at 455 nm in air. Our results indicate a wavelength dependence of laser-induced optical damage in bichromatic cavities and provide an estimate of the blue light intensity that can be safely used in such cavities.
tldr: The paper experimentally studies wavelength-dependent finesse degradation and partial recovery in a bichromatic high-finesse optical cavity under vacuum and continuous laser illumination.
motivation: High-finesse optical cavities used in cavity QED and related experiments must remain stable under vacuum and high circulating power, especially when multiple wavelengths are used for stabilization, trapping, and light-matter coupling.
method: Cavity ring-down measurements are performed on a bichromatic cavity with high-reflectivity coatings at 455 nm and 671 nm, comparing degradation under blue and red resonant illumination and modeling the loss kinetics with oxygen-depletion and Avrami-type models.
result: The 455 nm finesse drops from 7.7×10^3 to 1.9×10^3 after 11 hours of high-power blue illumination, while the 671 nm finesse shows no measurable degradation; red illumination alone causes no measurable degradation at either wavelength, and partial blue finesse recovery is observed after illumination in air.
conclusion: Laser-induced optical damage in this bichromatic cavity is wavelength-dependent, and the results provide an estimate of safe blue-light intensity for such cavities, though the microscopic degradation mechanism is not uniquely identified.

title: Phase-space Dynamics And Multicomponent Wave-packet Structures In The Dunkl Anharmonic Oscillator
authors: R. D. Mota D. Ojeda-Guill\'en
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the phase-space dynamics and multicomponent wave-packet structures of the Dunkl anharmonic oscillator (Kerr medium). Starting from the time-evolved state, we derive analytical expressions for the Dunkl-Husimi [MATH]-function and a normalized angular Husimi profile. The Dunkl parameter modifies the coherent-state excitation weights and the parity-dependent phase accumulation, producing angular anisotropy and asymmetric phase-space separation. For the half-integer deformation [MATH], the dynamics generate asymmetric multicomponent Husimi patterns with unequal peak heights and an early reconstruction at [MATH]. For the deformation [MATH], the Husimi distribution exhibits broadening while retaining its multimodal structure and unitary evolution. At the fundamental nonlinear revival time, the wave packet is reconstructed for the selected parameter ratio. The standard Kerr dynamics are recovered in the limit [MATH].
tldr: The paper analytically studies phase-space dynamics and multicomponent wave-packet structures of a Dunkl-deformed anharmonic oscillator/Kerr medium using Dunkl-Husimi distributions.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize how the Dunkl deformation modifies coherent-state dynamics, phase-space distributions, and wave-packet revival structures in a nonlinear oscillator model.
method: They derive analytical expressions for the Dunkl-Husimi function and a normalized angular Husimi profile from the time-evolved state, focusing on half-integer and integer deformation parameters.
result: The Dunkl parameter changes excitation weights and parity-dependent phases, producing angular anisotropy, asymmetric multicomponent Husimi patterns, early reconstruction, and broadening while preserving multimodal unitary evolution.
conclusion: The Dunkl anharmonic oscillator exhibits deformation-controlled phase-space signatures and revival behavior, with standard Kerr dynamics recovered in the undeformed limit.

title: Scaling Laws For Parameter Setting In Digitized Counterdiabatic Qaoa
authors: Jiapei Zhuang Yaocheng Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimizing parameters separately for each problem instance limits the reuse of variational quantum algorithms. We develop empirical scaling laws for parameter setting in the digitized counterdiabatic quantum approximate optimization algorithm (DC-QAOA) for weighted MaxCut. The prescription combines exact covariance under uniform edge-weight rescaling with power laws in mean degree fitted separately to offline-optimized cost and counterdiabatic angles. After the weight and degree scales are removed, the optimized angles of different training graphs cluster around common amplitudes, so a small coefficient table suffices. Frozen coefficients assign angles from a target graph's mean degree and root-mean-square edge weight without target-instance variational optimization. In ideal-circuit simulations across 1050 test graphs spanning ten graph families and five positive edge-weight distributions, mean optimal-solution probability is higher than that of the fixed-angle quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) at each depth from one to four layers, reaching 19.36% versus 13.11% at four layers. A six-layer extension on 600 graphs also shows a mean probability advantage. Hardware execution on the IBM Quantum processor ibm_fez for 21 unit-weight 3-regular graphs shows a mean probability advantage at one layer, while the ordering reverses at two layers. In separate energy-based experiments, direct assignment gives a higher mean approximation ratio than random-start optimization reaches within 500 evaluations, and refinement started from the formula angles improves it further. These results show how a scaling-based representation of optimized angles can guide parameter reuse across graph instances, enabling direct parameter assignment without target-instance variational optimization and providing initial angles for local refinement.
tldr: The paper develops empirical scaling laws for directly assigning parameters in digitized counterdiabatic QAOA for weighted MaxCut, avoiding per-instance variational optimization.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms typically require costly instance-specific parameter optimization, limiting reusability and scalability across problem instances.
method: The authors fit power laws in mean graph degree for offline-optimized cost and counterdiabatic angles, remove weight and degree scaling, and use a small coefficient table to assign angles from target graph statistics; they test in ideal simulations and on IBM hardware.
result: Frozen coefficient assignment outperforms fixed-angle QAOA in ideal simulations across many graphs and depths, with mean optimal-solution probability reaching 19.36% versus 13.11% at four layers, and shows mixed hardware results.
conclusion: Scaling-based angle representations can enable parameter reuse and direct assignment for DC-QAOA, providing good initial angles for local refinement without target-instance optimization.

title: Implications Of The Pxp Ground-state Sign Structure For Neural-network Variational Monte Carlo
authors: Kwangmin Yu Jun Sur Richard Park
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Positive-definite neural-network quantum states cannot directly represent the ground state of the PXP Hamiltonian, since the ground-state wavefunction carries a nontrivial relative-sign structure. Building on the chiral symmetry of the PXP Hamiltonian, we show that this sign structure is fixed exactly by the parity of the total up-spin number: a diagonal unitary transformation that assigns a sign to each spin configuration according to this parity maps the PXP Hamiltonian to its negative, rendering the transformed Hamiltonian stoquastic on the Rydberg-blockaded Hilbert space. Since the configuration graph of allowed configurations is connected, the Perron-Frobenius theorem guarantees a unique, strictly positive ground state of the transformed Hamiltonian, yielding an exact sign rule for the ground state of the original Hamiltonian in terms of the parity of the up-spin number. Variational Monte Carlo performed directly on the transformed Hamiltonian with a positive-definite ansatz therefore requires no architecture-specific modification to represent the true ground state. We evaluate the performance of this formulation using five representative neural-network quantum state architectures, SineKAN, reflection-symmetrized SineKAN, RBM, MLP, and LSTM, for different chain lengths.
tldr: The paper derives an exact ground-state sign rule for the PXP Hamiltonian based on up-spin parity and uses it to enable positive-definite neural-network variational Monte Carlo on a stoquastic transformed Hamiltonian.
motivation: Positive-definite neural-network quantum states cannot directly represent the nontrivial relative-sign structure of the PXP ground state, motivating an exact sign rule that avoids architecture-specific modifications.
method: Using the chiral symmetry of the PXP Hamiltonian, the authors construct a diagonal unitary transformation that maps the Hamiltonian to its negative and makes it stoquastic on the connected Rydberg-blockaded Hilbert space; Perron-Frobenius then guarantees a positive ground state. They benchmark five neural-network architectures on the transformed problem.
result: The ground-state sign structure is fixed exactly by the parity of the total up-spin number, and variational Monte Carlo with a positive-definite ansatz can represent the true ground state without architecture changes. Performance is evaluated for SineKAN, reflection-symmetrized SineKAN, RBM, MLP, and LSTM across chain lengths.
conclusion: The work provides a useful exact sign rule and practical VMC formulation for the PXP model, but it lies outside the researcher's core directions in quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Confinement Geometry Regulates Fluctuations, Densities, And Collective Escape In Interacting Active Matter
authors: Sandipan Dutta Renu Parashar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active matter exhibits non-equilibrium signatures such as the violation of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, giant number fluctuations, and non-Gaussian velocity distributions. We investigate how confinement geometry and particle number influence the steady-state behavior of sterically interacting Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particles (AOUPs) in a double-well potential. Unlike bulk active systems, increasing particle number suppresses non-equilibrium fluctuations through crowding, making the steady-state density profiles increasingly resemble those of passive systems. Nevertheless, instantaneous active density profiles exhibit both unimodal and bimodal distributions, even at large particle numbers, whereas passive profiles remain bimodal. The local velocity and position distributions are unimodal in the concave regions of the potential but become bimodal in non-concave regions. Confinement suppresses long-range correlations while producing spatially localized fluctuations governed by potential geometry. Velocity fluctuations are suppressed in the densely populated wells but enhanced near the barrier, where non-equilibrium effects are strongest. At large persistence times, correlated barrier crossings and strong velocity-alignment correlations emerge, which are absent in passive systems. These results demonstrate how confinement geometry, crowding, and persistence jointly control density fluctuations, velocity correlations, and collective escape in interacting active matter.
tldr: The paper studies how confinement geometry, crowding, and persistence control density and velocity fluctuations and collective barrier crossing in sterically interacting Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles confined in a double-well potential.
motivation: Active matter displays non-equilibrium signatures such as fluctuation-dissipation violation and giant number fluctuations, but how confinement geometry and particle number jointly shape steady-state behavior of interacting active particles is not well understood.
method: Numerical/simulation study of sterically interacting Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particles (AOUPs) in a double-well potential, varying particle number, persistence time, and confinement geometry, with analysis of density profiles, local velocity/position distributions, and spatial correlations.
result: Increasing particle number suppresses non-equilibrium fluctuations via crowding, making steady-state densities resemble passive systems, while instantaneous active profiles can be unimodal or bimodal; velocity fluctuations are suppressed in dense wells but enhanced near barriers, and at large persistence times correlated barrier crossings and velocity-alignment correlations emerge that are absent passively.
conclusion: Confinement geometry, crowding, and persistence jointly govern density fluctuations, velocity correlations, and collective escape in interacting active matter, distinguishing it from bulk active and passive systems.

title: Iterative Quantum Optimization: From Greedy Reductions To Branch-and-Bound
authors: Stuart Hadfield, Lucas T. Braydwood, Eleanor Rieffel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Iterative quantum optimization (IQO) uses quantum-generated information to select a sequence of classical problem reductions. We introduce Bound-Aware Tree-IQO which combines this iterative structure with bounds and reversible search. Feasible measured samples update a shared incumbent, while valid classical bounds prune branches that cannot improve it. Incorporating backtracking yields an anytime method that returns the best feasible solution found when interrupted, or can be run as a complete search to return and certify the optimum. For suitable single-variable or pairwise reductions, an initial IQO path can determine the branching schedule without further quantum calls, though certifying the optimum may take superpolynomial classical time. To motivate our framework, we prove two limitations of irreversible IQO reductions based on the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). We show an infinite family of unweighted MaxCut instances on which globally optimized level-1 QAOA makes standard Recursive QAOA strictly prefer a first reduction that excludes every optimal solution, and limits that branch to an approximation ratio of at most [MATH]. In contrast, a single backtrack recovers an optimal solution using the same quantum information. Causal cone arguments give a complementary obstruction at every fixed depth of standard QAOA: a weighted MaxCut instance is shown to contain two edges with identical two-qubit reduced states, even though every optimum requires opposite edge parities. MaxCut experiments show that QAOA-guided ordering is nonrandom in exact-certification tests through [MATH], while demonstrating that quantum samples can strengthen the incumbent and enable further pruning. Our results suggest that quantum data could provide useful guidance toward solving hard combinatorial optimization problems more effectively than either quantum or classical algorithms alone.
tldr: The paper introduces Bound-Aware Tree-IQO, an anytime branch-and-bound framework that uses quantum-generated samples to guide classical problem reductions for combinatorial optimization.
motivation: Iterative quantum optimization can use quantum information to select classical reductions, but irreversible reduction choices may discard optimal solutions; the authors aim to add bounds and reversibility to avoid such failures.
method: They combine IQO with classical bounds, incumbent updates, reversible search, and backtracking, and prove limitations of standard Recursive QAOA reductions using MaxCut constructions and causal-cone arguments.
result: They show an infinite family of unweighted MaxCut instances where level-1 QAOA-guided Recursive QAOA strictly excludes all optimal solutions in its first reduction, while a single backtrack recovers optimality; MaxCut experiments demonstrate nonrandom QAOA-guided ordering and pruning benefits.
conclusion: Quantum samples may provide useful guidance for hard combinatorial optimization when embedded in a bound-aware reversible search framework, outperforming either purely quantum or classical approaches alone.

title: Weak-coupling Selection And Finite-torus Entropy In The Triangular Ising Antiferromagnet
authors: Pengcheng Hou Weiqi Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An antiferromagnetic second-neighbor interaction favors stripe order in the triangular-lattice Ising antiferromagnet, but uniform stripes cannot satisfy odd periodic boundaries. At each fixed odd size [MATH], we minimize this interaction over the ground states of the zero-field nearest-neighbor model on an [MATH] torus. We prove a minimum total interface length of [MATH] and classify all [MATH] selected states. Under the uniform measure on these states, the area fractions of the three stripe orientations approach a uniform distribution over all nonnegative triples summing to one. Thus selection reduces an exponential degeneracy to polynomial growth, while the whole-sample orientation fractions remain broadly distributed. We also derive explicit two-sided entropy-density bounds for periodic spin ground states and honeycomb dimer coverings on [MATH] tori, where [MATH] are the periods along the two primitive lattice directions. For all [MATH], the errors relative to the bulk residual entropy are bounded by explicit constants times [MATH], without an aspect-ratio restriction. These bounds give finite-size accuracy guarantees and control the exponentially small fraction of unperturbed ground states that survive the selection.
tldr: The paper studies ground-state selection and finite-torus entropy bounds for the triangular-lattice Ising antiferromagnet with weak second-neighbor interactions.
motivation: Second-neighbor antiferromagnetic interactions favor stripe order on the triangular lattice, but odd periodic boundaries frustrate uniform stripes; the authors aim to characterize which ground states are selected and how finite-size entropy behaves.
method: They minimize the second-neighbor interaction over zero-field nearest-neighbor ground states on odd-by-odd tori, prove a minimum interface-length result, classify selected states, and derive explicit two-sided entropy-density bounds for periodic spin ground states and honeycomb dimer coverings.
result: The selected states reduce an exponential ground-state degeneracy to polynomial growth, while orientation fractions remain broadly distributed; entropy-density bounds have explicit finite-size error controls without aspect-ratio restrictions.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous finite-size entropy bounds and a classification of weak-coupling selection in a frustrated classical Ising antiferromagnet, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Beef: A Hybrid Integrated Photonic Simulation Framework
authors: Stephen E. Ralph Jacob M. Hiesener
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Python framework is presented that retains first-principles electromagnetic modeling while extending simulation to devices whose length and geometric complexity place them beyond the practical reach of either method alone. The Bridged Engine for eigenmode expansion (EME) and finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) (BEEF) partitions a device into sections which are simulated using either EME or FDTD independently developed Maxwell solvers depending on what best suits each section's geometry, and cascades the resulting responses. BEEF calibrates the EME propagation constants against FDTD-measured phase accumulation, providing a mode identity verification diagnostic across solver interfaces. For a 2x2 multimode-interference splitter, the hybrid result agrees with full-device FDTD to within 0.59% (bar) and 0.76% (cross) across the C-band; a tapered variant agrees to within 0.87% and 2.01%, respectively. For a directional coupler, effective-index calibration reduces cut-position dependence 167-fold. A circuit-level cascade reproduces the measured Fabry-Perot resonance lineshape and free spectral range while exploring the coupler-length and arm-length design plane through post-processing of four cached simulations. Finally, we use BEEF to simulate a 167.3 um-long 4x4 MMI-based 90-degree optical hybrid that is computationally impractical for full-device FDTD, with a reduced-length variant confirming close agreement in transmission and relative phase.
tldr: BEEF is a hybrid Python simulation framework that partitions photonic devices into sections solved by either eigenmode expansion (EME) or finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) and cascades the results, enabling first-principles modeling of long, geometrically complex integrated photonic devices.
motivation: Full-device FDTD is computationally prohibitive for long or complex photonic structures, while EME alone struggles with arbitrary geometries; a framework combining both solvers could extend rigorous Maxwell modeling to device scales previously out of reach.
method: The device is segmented and each section is simulated with whichever solver (EME or FDTD) suits its geometry, with S-matrix cascading of the responses; EME propagation constants are calibrated against FDTD-measured phase accumulation, and a mode-identity diagnostic verifies consistency across solver interfaces.
result: For a 2x2 MMI splitter the hybrid result matches full-device FDTD to within 0.59% (bar) and 0.76% (cross) over the C-band (0.87% and 2.01% for a tapered variant), effective-index calibration reduces directional-coupler cut-position dependence 167-fold, and a 167.3 um 4x4 MMI-based 90-degree optical hybrid is simulated where full FDTD is impractical.
conclusion: Hybrid EME/FDTD partitioning with cross-solver calibration delivers accurate, computationally tractable simulation of large integrated photonic circuits, offering a practical design tool for classical photonic components.

title: Nonperturbative Theory Of Thin-vapor-layer Linear Optical Properties: Towards The Optimal Design Of Alkali-metal Vapor Nanocells
authors: Tigran A. Vartanyan Andrei V. Ermolaev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hot alkali-metal vapors confined inside nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells are highly suitable media for miniature and cheap frequency standards, magnetometers and atomic sensors. Yet, their linear optical properties in case of low to moderate atomic densities are not fully understood. The primary reason for that is the complex, strongly nonlocal optical response of such systems to the incident resonant radiation arising as the result of the free motion of atoms and their collisions with the walls. To date, calculations of reflection and transmission spectra of these cells has been restricted to perturbation theory in atomic density for the case of quenching atom-wall collisions, which substantially limited the scope of their practical applications. Here we introduce the rigorous numerical approach for computing thin-vapor-layer spectra with an accurate account for the nonlocal optical response at arbitrary optical density and layer thickness. Our model predicts a density-dependent blue shift of the resonance that is absent in the first-order perturbative description. We show that its values are comparable to the natural linewidth of an atomic transition and, therefore, too large to be neglected in most use cases. Inspired by recent experiments, we then explore a wide range of vapor layer thicknesses and study how the reflectivity and its derivative with respect to the laser detuning depend on the layer thickness. Finally, we derive an approximate expression for the thickness at which the first derivative of the reflectivity reaches its maximum that agrees closely with the rigorous numerical model and reduces to the first-order analytical result. These results provide a practical design tool for nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells in different applications as well as a starting point for further development of the theory.
tldr: A nonperturbative numerical theory of the linear optical response of nanometer-thick alkali-metal vapor layers, used to guide the design of vapor nanocells for atomic sensors and frequency standards.
motivation: Thin vapor cells are promising cheap platforms for miniature frequency standards, magnetometers, and atomic sensors, but their reflection and transmission spectra were only understood perturbatively in atomic density and only for quenching atom-wall collisions, limiting practical design.
method: The authors develop a rigorous numerical approach that accounts for the nonlocal optical response arising from free atomic motion and wall collisions at arbitrary optical density and layer thickness, and use it to scan layer thicknesses and compute reflectivity and its detuning derivative.
result: The model predicts a density-dependent blue shift of the resonance absent at first order, comparable to the natural linewidth, and yields an approximate analytic expression for the thickness maximizing the first derivative of reflectivity that matches the numerical results and reduces to the perturbative limit.
conclusion: The work provides a practical design tool for nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells and a foundation for further development of the theory of nonlocal vapor-layer optics.

title: Ultra-broadband Quantum Infrared Spectroscopy Extending To 20 {\textmu}m
authors: Yu Mukai, Ryo Okamoto, Shigeki Takeuchi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum infrared spectroscopy (QIRS), which exploits quantum interference between photon-pair generation processes, enables infrared spectroscopy using only visible and near-infrared (VNIR) light sources and detectors. Extending the spectral coverage of QIRS into the long-wavelength infrared region up to 20 {\textmu}m is crucial for the identification and characterization of a broad range of materials. However, implementing QIRS beyond 10 {\textmu}m has been challenging because the nonlinear materials used to date do not provide suitable photon-pair sources in this spectral region. Here, we design a wavelength-tunable photon-pair source based on a gallium selenide crystal and develop a QIRS system covering a broad spectral range from 8.6 to 20 {\textmu}m. Using this system, we measure the transmittance spectrum of a polystyrene film and observe characteristic absorption bands beyond 10 {\textmu}m relevant to identifying polystyrene and to probing local chain conformation. These results demonstrate that QIRS is capable of covering the entire molecular fingerprint region.
tldr: The paper demonstrates ultra-broadband quantum infrared spectroscopy up to 20 μm using a gallium selenide-based wavelength-tunable photon-pair source.
motivation: Extending quantum infrared spectroscopy beyond 10 μm is important for identifying a wide range of materials in the molecular fingerprint region, but suitable photon-pair sources have been lacking.
method: The authors design a wavelength-tunable photon-pair source based on a gallium selenide crystal and build a quantum infrared spectroscopy system covering 8.6–20 μm.
result: They measure the transmittance spectrum of a polystyrene film and observe characteristic absorption bands beyond 10 μm relevant to material identification and local chain conformation.
conclusion: The work shows that quantum infrared spectroscopy can cover the entire molecular fingerprint region, enabling infrared spectroscopy with visible/near-infrared light sources and detectors.

title: Energy-Centroid Trembling Near Exceptional Points In Photonic Time Crystals
authors: Kyungmin Lee, Younsung Kim, Minwook Kyung, Seungmin Yeon, Bumki Min
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a photonic time crystal with a modulated Lorentz restoring coefficient, modulation reweights the potential energy of the polarization and loss drains its kinetic energy; when these sectors are offset within a pulse, the energy centroid trembles in every cycle while the Poynting-flux velocity stays bounded. Near the gap-edge exceptional point the mode geometry amplifies these offsets, and for a narrow-band pulse on one passband Floquet branch the trembling-velocity amplitude generically grows as the inverse square root of the momentum detuning, rounded by finite bandwidth. Loss modulated in phase or in antiphase with the restoring coefficient can change the trembling coefficient while the band-slope and Petermann coefficients barely move. In the lossy example studied, a forward field pulse launched with the polarization at rest exhibits delayed bursts near the beat recurrence after substantial energy loss, with monochromatic amplitudes following the inverse three-halves power of the detuning over the computed range. Intracycle energy exchange and preparation thus shape the centroid motion beyond what the band slope and the Floquet Petermann factor determine.
tldr: The paper analyzes energy-centroid trembling in a lossy photonic time crystal near exceptional points, showing that intracycle energy exchange and mode geometry affect pulse energy dynamics beyond standard Floquet band-slope and Petermann-factor descriptions.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how modulated loss and restoring coefficients in a photonic time crystal reshape energy transport near gap-edge exceptional points, especially when potential and kinetic energy sectors are offset within a pulse.
method: They study a photonic time crystal with a modulated Lorentz restoring coefficient, use Floquet passband branches and detuning scaling, and examine how in-phase or antiphase loss modulation alters the trembling coefficient relative to band-slope and Petermann coefficients.
result: Near the exceptional point, the trembling-velocity amplitude generically scales as the inverse square root of momentum detuning, rounded by finite bandwidth; in a lossy example, delayed bursts appear near beat recurrence with monochromatic amplitudes following an inverse three-halves power of detuning.
conclusion: Intracycle energy exchange and pulse preparation significantly shape centroid motion, so band slope and Floquet Petermann factor alone do not fully determine the energy-centroid dynamics.

title: Beyond Typical Strings: Sampling The Complexity Landscape
authors: Abdurrahman Hadi Erturk, Joshua Sharkey, Nora S Martin, Kamal Dingle, Ard A Louis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uniform random sampling of strings is overwhelmingly dominated by high-complexity strings, leaving the much smaller set of low- and intermediate-complexity strings largely unexplored. Here, we adapt the nested neutral set estimator (NNSE), a Monte Carlo rare-event sampling method, to estimate the distribution P(K) of complexity values for binary strings of fixed length. NNSE allows us to explore the full complexity landscape, including exponentially rare low-complexity regions that are inaccessible to direct sampling, for string lengths up to several hundred. We apply the method to several widely used complexity measures: Lempel-Ziv 76 (LZ76), Lempel-Ziv 78 (LZ78), context tree weighting (CTW), the block decomposition method (BDM), and block entropy. We further introduce uniform complexity weighting (UCW), which gives equal weight to different complexity levels rather than to individual strings. This approach provides a dataset-independent framework for comparing complexity measures across their full range and reveals substantial differences between measures for low- and intermediate-complexity strings that are largely hidden by conventional uniform sampling. Using the NNSE to perform UCW sampling allows us to compare complexity measures across their full range in a dataset-independent way. This reveals differences in their behavior for low- and intermediate-complexity strings that are practically inaccessible to conventional uniform sampling.
tldr: The paper introduces a rare-event sampling method to estimate the distribution of complexity values for binary strings and compares several classical complexity measures across the full complexity landscape.
motivation: Uniform random sampling is dominated by high-complexity strings, so low- and intermediate-complexity strings remain poorly explored and complexity measures are hard to compare fairly across their full range.
method: The authors adapt the nested neutral set estimator (NNSE), a Monte Carlo rare-event sampling technique, to sample binary strings by complexity and estimate P(K) for LZ76, LZ78, CTW, BDM, and block entropy; they also introduce uniform complexity weighting (UCW).
result: NNSE accesses exponentially rare low-complexity regions for strings up to several hundred bits, and UCW reveals substantial differences between complexity measures at low and intermediate complexity that are hidden under conventional uniform sampling.
conclusion: The work provides a dataset-independent framework for comparing classical complexity measures over their full range and highlights the importance of rare low-complexity strings.

title: Noise Stability On The Hypercube: Order $7/8$
authors: Lei Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a balanced Boolean function [MATH] on the discrete hypercube, we study the [MATH]-stability [MATH], where [MATH] is the Boolean noise operator and [MATH]. Using the asymmetric Hellinger kernel estimates recently established by OpenAI, we prove that dictators minimize the [MATH]-stability in every dimension and at every correlation [MATH]. At interior correlations they are the only minimizers. As a consequence, dictators minimize the [MATH]-stability for every [MATH], maximize the [MATH]-stability for every [MATH], and maximize the one-sided Shannon entropy stability [MATH]. This resolves a conjecture of Li and M\'edard and strengthens the Courtade--Kumar conjecture in the balanced setting.

motivation: Noise stability and entropy stability of Boolean functions are central in classical Boolean function analysis and information theory, with conjectures connecting optimal functions to dictators.
method: The author uses recently established asymmetric Hellinger kernel estimates to analyze the Boolean noise operator and prove extremal properties at all correlations.
result: Dictators are shown to minimize the relevant stability at every dimension and correlation, and to be unique minimizers at interior correlations; consequences include maximizing one-sided Shannon entropy stability and strengthening Courtade-Kumar in the balanced case.
conclusion: This is a significant classical functional-analysis/information-theory result but has no direct quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems content.

title: Nonnegative Rank Bounds For The Algebraic Monotone Calculus
authors: Fedor Part
abstract: ArXiv:2611.01055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Hrubes' Algebraic Monotone Calculus a DNF tautology [MATH] is proved by a monotone arithmetic circuit computing [MATH] for some [MATH], where the coefficient of [MATH] at [MATH] counts the terms of [MATH] satisfied by [MATH], and [MATH]. Proof size is circuit size, and [MATH] is existentially quantified, so lower bounds must hold at arbitrarily small [MATH]. We prove lower bounds for bounded-depth fragments by two nonnegative rank measures of the target: monotone tensor rank and the nonnegative rank of a flattening. At depth three a proof is a nonnegative tensor decomposition. Restricting its terms to subcube indicators gives conical juntas, a system polynomially equivalent to Sherali-Adams in twin variables. For arbitrary terms we adapt Rothvoss' hyperplane separation to monotone tensor rank: Tseitin formulas on constant-degree expanders of large girth need proofs of size [MATH] whenever [MATH]. This cannot reach every [MATH]: at shift [MATH] Tseitin acquires polynomial-size depth-three proofs, separating the two fragments exponentially. A constant-size index gadget gives bounds for every [MATH], converting a Sherali-Adams degree bound into a size bound. Depth three is essential: Tseitin has monotone proofs of size [MATH] and depth [MATH] at every [MATH]. Beyond depth three we bound the nonnegative rank of a flattening by [MATH] for a monotone formula with [MATH] leaves and mixed-product depth [MATH]: the largest number of product gates on a root-to-leaf path whose two inputs each meet both sides of the bipartition. Approximate extension complexity then bounds perfect matching and odd factor instances, and planted CSP integrality gaps give an explicit family of planted Tseitin DNFs hard at inverse-polynomial shift.
tldr: The paper proves lower bounds on proof size in Hrubes' Algebraic Monotone Calculus using nonnegative rank measures — monotone tensor rank and the nonnegative rank of a flattening — for bounded-depth fragments, including Tseitin formulas on expanders and perfect matching instances.
motivation: Proof-size lower bounds in algebraic proof systems are hard because the parameter in the monotone calculus is existentially quantified and must hold at arbitrarily small values, so new rank-based measures are needed to attack bounded-depth fragments.
method: The authors introduce monotone tensor rank and nonnegative rank of a flattening as lower-bound measures, connect depth-three proofs to nonnegative tensor decompositions/conical juntas equivalent to Sherali-Adams in twin variables, and adapt Rothvoss' hyperplane separation argument to monotone tensor rank.
result: Tseitin formulas on constant-degree large-girth expanders require exponentially large depth-three proofs for small enough values of the parameter, yet acquire polynomial-size depth-three proofs at a larger value, exponentially separating fragments; constant-size index gadgets extend bounds to all values, and approximate extension complexity bounds perfect matching and odd factor instances.
conclusion: Nonnegative-rank techniques yield strong depth-sensitive lower bounds in the algebraic monotone calculus, showing depth three is essential and connecting monotone proof complexity to extension complexity and Sherali-Adams degree bounds.

title: Painlev\'e Vi Superintegrability And Heun-Racah Algebras
authors: Sarah Post Ian Marquette
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the two fourth-order quantum superintegrable systems in the Euclidean plane that separate in polar coordinates and whose angular potentials are determined by the general four-parameter sixth Painlev\'e transcendent. One system has an oscillator radial term and the other an extended-Coulomb radial term. For both systems we give the fourth-order quantum integral explicitly, derive the cubic symmetry algebra and its Casimir, and construct a deformed-oscillator realization. At fixed energy the two algebras are specializations of the Heun--Racah algebra. Their structure functions contain the same quartic angular factor, determined by the Painlev\'e~VI parameters, while different radial factors distinguish oscillator and Coulomb dynamics. The Coulomb integral is obtained by transforming the Cartesian Hermitian symmetry at the operator level. The lower-order terms generated by the polar coordinate change are essential for commutation with the Hamiltonian. The two quantum systems are also related by the Levi-Civita transformation and coupling-constant metamorphosis, which gives a direct correspondence between their Painlev\'e parameters, algebras, Casimirs and representations. Earlier exceptional-Jacobi models arise at special rational parameter values, whereas the results here apply to the full four-parameter Painlev\'e~VI family. We also compare the quantum results with the corresponding classical Poisson algebras.
tldr: The paper constructs fourth-order quantum superintegrable systems in the Euclidean plane whose angular potentials are governed by the Painlevé VI transcendent, and analyzes their cubic symmetry and Heun-Racah algebras.
motivation: The authors aim to extend superintegrability and algebraic symmetry results from exceptional-Jacobi models to the full four-parameter Painlevé VI family.
method: They explicitly derive fourth-order quantum integrals, cubic symmetry algebras and Casimirs, deformed-oscillator realizations, and use Levi-Civita transformations and coupling-constant metamorphosis to relate oscillator and Coulomb systems.
result: Both systems yield Heun-Racah algebras at fixed energy with structure functions sharing a Painlevé-VI-determined quartic angular factor but differing radial factors, and earlier exceptional-Jacobi cases appear at special rational parameters.
conclusion: The work provides a unified algebraic treatment of Painlevé VI superintegrable quantum systems and clarifies their classical and quantum symmetry structures.

title: Experimental Demonstration Of Response-enhanced Fiber Sagnac Gyroscopy Via Imaginary Weak-value Amplification
authors: Jing-Hui Huang, Hong-Liang Cui, Tianying Chang, Jing Zhang, Tianye Huang, Xiang-Yun Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally demonstrate a 100-m long fiber Sagnac gyroscope employing imaginary weak-value amplification (IWVA) to enhance the optical readout response to rotation. A Sagnac-induced polarization phase is converted into a measurable spectral response through polarization post-selection and spectrally resolved detection. By varying the post-selection angle, we characterize the gyroscope response over the experimentally accessible rotation-rate range. The response increases systematically toward orthogonal post-selection, yielding a maximum experimental enhancement of approximately 13 times relative to a fixed reference configuration without postselection. Fast Fourier transform and Allan-deviation measurements further characterize the noise and stability of the gyroscope. Near-orthogonal post-selection reduces the equivalent rotation-rate fluctuations, with the minimum Allan deviation decreasing from [MATH] for the reference configuration to [MATH] for the configuration exhibiting the maximum response enhancement, corresponding to an approximately 6.6-fold reduction. Low-frequency fluctuations of the broadband superluminescent diode source limit the long-term stability. These results demonstrate that IWVA provides a practical approach for response-enhanced fiber-based Sagnac gyroscopy and precision rotation sensing.
tldr: The authors experimentally demonstrate a 100 m fiber Sagnac gyroscope that uses imaginary weak-value amplification to enhance rotation readout.
motivation: Fiber Sagnac gyroscopes require high sensitivity to rotation, and weak-value amplification is explored as a practical method to improve optical readout response.
method: A Sagnac-induced polarization phase is converted into a spectral response via polarization post-selection and spectrally resolved detection; response and noise are characterized versus post-selection angle using FFT and Allan deviation.
result: Near-orthogonal post-selection yields about 13× response enhancement relative to a reference configuration and reduces minimum Allan deviation by about 6.6×, though broadband source fluctuations limit long-term stability.
conclusion: Imaginary weak-value amplification is shown to be a practical approach for response-enhanced fiber Sagnac gyroscopy and precision rotation sensing.

title: Large $n$ Limit Of The Ratio Of Lukyanov Integrals
authors: Dong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the large-[MATH] asymptotics of ratios of Lukyanov integrals for fixed real coupling [MATH]. Our approach uses their biorthogonal ensemble structure and vector Riemann--Hilbert techniques. Under stated analytic hypotheses, we derive the logarithmic ratio through its constant term, which is expressed by a Fredholm determinant. The expansion is locally uniform in the real parameter [MATH] and is formulated separately for even and odd particle numbers. We verify the hypotheses for the correction defined by the physical ground-state thermodynamic Bethe ansatz. The relation to quantum-field-theoretic one-point functions is discussed separately.
tldr: The paper derives large-n asymptotics for ratios of Lukyanov integrals using biorthogonal ensembles and vector Riemann-Hilbert methods.
motivation: Ratios of Lukyanov integrals appear in integrable models and thermodynamic Bethe ansatz contexts, motivating a detailed asymptotic analysis.
method: The author exploits the biorthogonal ensemble structure of the integrals and applies vector Riemann-Hilbert techniques to obtain a Fredholm-determinant expression for the constant term.
result: Under analytic hypotheses, the logarithmic ratio is expanded locally uniformly in a real coupling parameter, separately for even and odd particle numbers, and the hypotheses are verified for a physical ground-state TBA correction.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous asymptotic expansion for Lukyanov integral ratios and discusses connections to quantum-field-theoretic one-point functions, but it is not aligned with the specified quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems directions.

title: Non-Hermitian Theory Of Surface Emitting Jackiw-Rebbi States
authors: Hangkai Fan, Mingzhao Song, Andrey Bogdanov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological interface states in open photonic systems combine spatial localization at domain walls with temporal confinement characterized by a radiative quality factor. Here, we develop a non-Hermitian Dirac formalism for surface-emitting Jackiw-Rebbi states in dielectric metagratings. We show how varying the local amplitude of the lattice perturbation shapes the complex Dirac mass profile, enabling control over the quality factors and far-field radiation patterns of the interface states, while preserving their topological character. Applying this framework to a metagrating with second-order Brillouin-zone folding, we design a spatially graded superlattice perturbation that supports interface states with quality factors exceeding 10[MATH] and Hermite-Gaussian beam emission. These results establish superlattice perturbations as a strategy for topological beam shaping and offer a route toward high-Q topological surface emitters.
tldr: The paper develops a non-Hermitian Dirac theory for surface-emitting Jackiw-Rebbi interface states in dielectric metagratings and uses graded superlattice perturbations to control their quality factors and far-field emission.
motivation: Topological interface states in open photonic systems can combine spatial localization with radiative confinement, but controlling their quality factors and emission patterns while preserving topological character remains a design challenge.
method: The authors introduce a non-Hermitian Dirac formalism with a complex mass profile for Jackiw-Rebbi states and apply it to a metagrating with second-order Brillouin-zone folding and a spatially graded superlattice perturbation.
result: They show that varying the local perturbation amplitude tunes the complex Dirac mass, enabling interface states with quality factors exceeding 10^5 and Hermite-Gaussian beam emission.
conclusion: Superlattice perturbations provide a strategy for topological beam shaping and a route toward high-Q topological surface emitters in photonic metagratings.

title: Intent-Bound Authorization For Cryptocurrency Withdrawals Under Backend Compromise
authors: Toqeer Ali Syed, Asadullah Abdullah Khan, Ali Akrama
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Binance's preliminary account of its October 2026 attack raises a custody question that key protection alone cannot answer: how can a provider prevent unauthorized withdrawals when an attacker controls a service permitted to request signatures? We propose the Intent-Bound Withdrawal Authorization Protocol (IWAP). Before signing, independent enforcement checks customer intent, exact transaction effects, fresh workload evidence, and a committed single-use spending reservation. Administrative actions use a separate authorization path. We specify the protocol's trust assumptions and give conditional arguments for intent preservation, replay resistance, and a fixed-epoch exposure bound. A Python reference monitor authenticates synthetic records with Ed25519 and serializes reservations with SQLite. It rejects 1,200 negative requests, accepts 3,000 valid synthetic requests, and preserves a 100-unit budget under 64 concurrent attempts in each of 20 trials. When the intent authority is deliberately compromised, malicious requests pass, but the independent budget still limits admitted exposure. The study evaluates a normalized policy model, not Binance's infrastructure or a deployed custody platform. Its contribution is an explicit authorization boundary and reproducible tests of that boundary.
tldr: The paper proposes IWAP, an intent-bound authorization protocol for cryptocurrency withdrawals that limits exposure when backend services are compromised.
motivation: Custody providers relying solely on key protection cannot stop an attacker who controls a service authorized to request signatures, as illustrated by the Binance October 2026 incident.
method: The protocol adds independent pre-signing enforcement of customer intent, exact transaction effects, fresh workload attestation, and a committed single-use spending reservation, with administrative actions on a separate path; a Python reference monitor using Ed25519 and SQLite is evaluated on synthetic records.
result: The monitor rejects all 1,200 negative requests, accepts 3,000 valid ones, and preserves a 100-unit budget across 64 concurrent attempts in 20 trials, while a compromised intent authority still yields bounded exposure via the independent budget.
conclusion: The work contributes an explicit authorization boundary with reproducible tests, but evaluates a normalized policy model rather than a deployed custody platform.

title: Animated Ultraviolet Holography Via Programmable Nonlinear Phase Transfer
authors: Ze Zheng, Olga Sergaeva, Davide Rocco, Luca Carletti, Can Tao, Yucheng Zhang, Guoquan Zhang, Costantino de Angelis, Lei Xu, Anatoly V. Zayats, Mohsen Rahmani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic and programmable control of ultraviolet (UV) light remains challenging because of conventional high material absorption and the limited functionality of optics such as lenses, mirrors or filters, and optoelectronic devices, such as spatial phase modulators, over the UV range. Here, by employing the concept of virtual metasurfaces based on arrays of programmable optical patterns on a 600-nm-thick lithium niobate film as the nonlinear medium, we demonstrate nonlinear phase transfer, generating programmable holography in the UV range. This arrangement provides a unique platform for generating animated holograms. A spatial light modulator encodes a computer-generated phase distribution onto a longer-wavelength pump beam, while second-harmonic generation transfers the programmed spatial phase to the UV field through the quadratic nonlinear interaction. Importantly, the nonlinear film serves as a simple frequency-conversion interface, eliminating the need for nanostructure patterning or direct UV spatial modulation. By incorporating the nonlinear phase relationship into the hologram design, we experimentally reconstruct six distinct UV holographic patterns, with normalised cross-correlation values ranging from 0.68 to 0.83, demonstrating reliable UV holographic image reconstruction. As a result, the dynamic updating of the SLM enables animated UV holograms at 10 Hz, demonstrating reconfigurable UV holography using the same nonlinear film. The system also supports tunable SHG emission from 350 to 390 nm and dynamic beam steering at approximately 20 Hz. The results demonstrate the potential of virtual metasurfaces to realise software-defined UV holography by transferring spatial programming across optical frequencies. This opens new opportunities for reconfigurable short-wavelength UV beam shaping and structured illumination, without the need for UV-compatible optics or optoelectronics.
tldr: The paper demonstrates programmable ultraviolet holography by encoding phase on a pump beam with a spatial light modulator and transferring it to UV light via second-harmonic generation in a thin lithium niobate film.
motivation: Dynamic UV beam shaping is difficult due to high material absorption and limited UV-compatible optical and optoelectronic components.
method: A computer-generated phase pattern is displayed on an SLM and imprinted onto a longer-wavelength pump; nonlinear second-harmonic generation in a 600-nm lithium niobate film transfers the spatial phase to the UV field.
result: Six distinct UV holographic patterns were reconstructed with normalized cross-correlation between 0.68 and 0.83, and animated UV holograms were shown at 10 Hz with tunable SHG from 350 to 390 nm.
conclusion: Virtual metasurfaces enable software-defined reconfigurable UV holography and beam steering without patterned nanostructures or direct UV spatial modulation.

title: Transient Subtraction Method: An Alternative Approach For Variance Reduction In Dissipative Particle Dynamics
authors: Xiaocheng Shang Xinyi Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The efficient and accurate computation of transport coefficients remains a numerical challenge in dissipative particle dynamics (DPD), which can require substantial sampling to control statistical uncertainty. We extend recent results obtained in Langevin dynamics to consider the transient subtraction method for reducing the variance of transport coefficient estimations in DPD. The system is initialised by perturbing equilibrium samples, and its relaxation towards equilibrium is monitored under the reference dynamics. A reference trajectory, initialised at equilibrium and driven by the same Brownian noise, provides a control variate for the transient response. We apply the transient subtraction method to the computation of the mobility and the shear viscosity in a Lennard-Jones fluid in DPD. The shear viscosity is obtained from the time-integrated response of a Fourier observable associated with the longitudinal velocity. Numerical comparisons with the naive transient estimator show that the transient subtraction method reduces the variance at various integration times, and the reduction is more pronounced with a higher friction coefficient. These results indicate that the transient subtraction method is able to improve the statistical precision of transport coefficient estimations in DPD and reduce the number of trajectories needed to attain a prescribed standard error.
tldr: The paper extends the transient subtraction method, a control-variate variance-reduction technique, to dissipative particle dynamics simulations for estimating mobility and shear viscosity in a Lennard-Jones fluid.
motivation: Accurate computation of transport coefficients in DPD requires enormous sampling to control statistical uncertainty, making variance reduction practically important for classical mesoscale simulation.
method: The system is initialized by perturbing equilibrium samples and its relaxation is monitored; a reference trajectory started at equilibrium and driven by the same Brownian noise serves as a control variate, and the approach is applied to mobility and shear viscosity via a Fourier observable of longitudinal velocity.
result: Numerical comparisons with the naive transient estimator show reduced variance at various integration times, with the improvement more pronounced at higher friction coefficients.
conclusion: The transient subtraction method improves statistical precision of transport coefficient estimates in DPD and reduces the number of trajectories needed to reach a prescribed standard error.

title: Nuclear Charge Radii From Precision Bound-Electron g-Factor Measurements
authors: Bastian Sikora
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An efficient method to determine absolute nuclear charge radii from high-precision bound-electron g-factor measurements in hydrogenlike ions is put forward. Assuming that a nuclear model independent radius determination is possible, we demonstrate that this method can improve the precision of the nuclear radius for several poorly known heavy isotopes by up to two orders of magnitude compared to current literature values, by utilizing recent breakthroughs in the quantum electrodynamics (QED) theory of the bound-electron g-factor [B. Sikora, V. A. Yerokhin, C. H. Keitel, and Z. Harman, Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 123001 (2025)]. This opens a new, independent pathway for testing nuclear structure models and resolving nuclear structure anomalies.
tldr: The paper proposes a method to extract absolute nuclear charge radii from precision bound-electron g-factor measurements in hydrogenlike ions, improving radius precision for poorly known heavy isotopes.
motivation: Nuclear charge radii are important for testing nuclear structure models, but many heavy isotopes have poorly known radii; precision QED calculations of bound-electron g-factors offer a possible independent determination pathway.
method: The author uses recent advances in the QED theory of bound-electron g-factors in hydrogenlike ions to infer nuclear charge radii, assuming a nuclear-model-independent radius determination is possible.
result: The method can improve the precision of nuclear radii for several poorly known heavy isotopes by up to two orders of magnitude compared with current literature values.
conclusion: This provides a new independent route for testing nuclear structure models and resolving nuclear structure anomalies, but it is outside quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Coherent Heat-bath Configuration Interaction With Many-body Perturbation Theory For Multivalent Atoms
authors: Shi-Cheng Yu, Zhen-Xiang Zhong, Cheng-Bin Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combinatorial growth of configuration-interaction spaces limits accurate calculations as the valence-electron number and orbital space increase. To reduce the size of the configuration-interaction space, we develop coherent heat-bath configuration interaction in a configuration-state-function basis and combine it with many-body perturbation theory. Configurations are selected by thresholding their coherent couplings to target wave functions, and a perturbative correction recovers residual valence correlation. For Al, a stringent threshold gives about 16-37 fold compression with excitation-energy deviations from the uncompressed calculations below 0.74 /cm; a looser threshold gives 63-113 fold compression with a maximum deviation of 18.22 /cm. For Si and P, roughly threefold to eightfold compression is achieved with maximum relative deviations of approximately 0.70% and 0.32%, respectively, for optical excitation energies. The perturbative correction improves the accuracy of all calculated total energies. These results support extending the method to high-precision calculations in more complex atomic systems.
tldr: The paper develops a coherent heat-bath configuration interaction method combined with many-body perturbation theory to compress configuration spaces for accurate atomic electronic-structure calculations.
motivation: Accurate configuration-interaction calculations become computationally prohibitive as valence-electron number and orbital spaces grow, motivating more efficient configuration-selection schemes.
method: The authors formulate coherent heat-bath configuration interaction in a configuration-state-function basis, select configurations by thresholding coherent couplings to target wave functions, and add a perturbative correction for residual valence correlation.
result: For Al, Si, and P, the method achieves substantial configuration-space compression while maintaining small deviations in excitation energies, and the perturbative correction improves total-energy accuracy.
conclusion: The approach enables more efficient high-precision atomic calculations and may be extended to more complex multivalent systems.

title: Multivariate Analogues Of Ruijsenaars' Hypergeometric Function

motivation: The work extends one-variable Ruijsenaars hypergeometric functions and nested multivariate Askey-Wilson functions to a hyperbolic modular-double setting.
method: It uses iterated coproducts and overlap coefficients between eigenfunctions of twisted primitive elements in representations of the modular double to build nested-product multivariate functions.

title: Analog And Hybrid Computing In The 21st Century
authors: Bernd Ulmann, Olivier Bournez, Corey J. Maley, Zhong Sun, Grace Li Zhang, Paul Manea, Michael D\"oll, Frank Delvigne, Alex J. H. Fedorec, Daniel Garza, Lucas Wetzel, Sara Obergassel, Pavol Pitonak, Christopher Jung, Daniel Thuerck, Mason A. Porter, Marcelo J. Rozenberg, Frederic Bergner, Bhaskar Choubey, Manyu Zhao, Ludovico Minati, Lucas B\"ottcher
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog computers solve problems through physical representations of mathematical variables and relations, often using the dynamics of electronic circuits and their associated signals. Many analog computers directly represent nonlinear dynamical systems; they encode their solutions in the signals that they generate. Although most modern scientific computing relies on digital architectures with inherently discrete-valued representations and algorithmic approaches, the design constraints of such architectures increasingly limit both performance and energy efficiency. Analog systems can circumvent some of these constraints; they execute specific computations very efficiently by mapping them directly onto physical processes using smaller and simpler computing elements than the ones in digital architectures. In this article, we provide an interdisciplinary perspective on modern analog and hybrid (i.e., analog-digital) computing. We discuss how modern scientific computing workflows can leverage analog approaches in various applications, such as in simulating dynamical systems, performing optimization, and enabling more energy-efficient implementations of artificial intelligence.
tldr: This article reviews modern analog and hybrid analog-digital computing, emphasizing physical representations of computation and applications in dynamical systems, optimization, and energy-efficient AI.
motivation: Digital architectures are increasingly limited by performance and energy constraints, motivating renewed interest in analog computing approaches that exploit physical dynamics directly.
method: The authors provide an interdisciplinary perspective on analog and hybrid computing, discussing circuit-level implementations, physical modeling of nonlinear systems, and application workflows.
result: The review highlights that analog systems can efficiently solve specific computations by mapping them onto physical processes using simpler and smaller elements than digital architectures.
conclusion: Analog and hybrid computing offer promising alternatives for certain scientific computing tasks, particularly where energy efficiency and direct physical simulation are critical.

title: Spatial Token Interleaving And Two-Pass Bp Decoding For Semantic Image Transmission
authors: Yifan Feng, Chentao Yue, Haiyao Yu, Gaoyang Pang, Xinyu Chen, Hao Chang, Branka Vucetic, Yonghui Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic error control coding (SECC) can correct the residual errors of a standard channel code with a foundation model that supplies a prior on the source content, but existing SECC schemes are designed for text. In this paper, we develop SECC for image transmission with spatial token interleaving and a two-pass belief propagation (BP) schedule. At the transmitter, a vector-quantized (VQ) tokenizer converts an image into tokens, which are transmitted in multiple low-density parity-check (LDPC) code blocks of fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR). In raster order, a block that BP fails to decode corrupts consecutive token rows, so the interleaver reorders the tokens such that adjacent tokens are carried by different blocks, without additional transmitted bits. At the receiver, after the first BP pass, token recovery fuses the token probabilities given by BP with the predictions of the autoregressive model Emu3-Gen, and the second BP pass decodes each block again with the fused distributions as priors on the information bits. On Kodak24 at 0.5 channel uses per pixel and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 0.15 dB, the second pass removes 92% of the token errors left by token recovery, and interleaving reduces the final token error rate by 88%. At medium to high SNR, the proposed receiver exceeds deep joint source--channel coding baselines with the same channel uses by at least 1.2 dB in peak signal-to-noise ratio.
tldr: The paper proposes a semantic error control coding scheme for image transmission using VQ tokens, spatial interleaving, and two-pass BP decoding with a foundation-model prior.
motivation: Existing semantic error control coding schemes are mainly designed for text, so the authors aim to extend them to image transmission over LDPC-coded 5G NR links.
method: Images are tokenized with a VQ tokenizer, interleaved across LDPC blocks to mitigate burst errors, and decoded with a two-pass BP schedule that fuses BP token probabilities with Emu3-Gen autoregressive predictions.
result: On Kodak24 at 0.5 channel uses per pixel and 0.15 dB SNR, the second BP pass removes 92% of residual token errors, while interleaving reduces the final token error rate by 88%; at medium-to-high SNR it outperforms deep JSCC baselines by at least 1.2 dB PSNR.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that foundation-model priors combined with interleaving and iterative BP decoding can significantly improve semantic image transmission reliability.

motivation: A recent preprint claims a subexponential-time algorithm for counting satisfying assignments of CNF formulas, which would refute ETH; this note examines whether the certified bounds ever yield a practical or even theoretical speed-up once constants are extracted.

title: Shared Randomness And Parallel Rounds In Permutation Sampling
authors: Haoxiang Huang

title: Optimal Conversion From Zero-Concentrated To Gaussian Differential Privacy
authors: Yu-Wei Chen, Aaradhya Pandey, Jordan Awan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.01218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) and zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) are two competing privacy accounting frameworks, but they share similar minimax lower bounds in various estimation problems. Moreover, it is known that a mechanism satisfying [MATH]-GDP satisfies [MATH]-zCDP, whereas the converse fails to hold at the same calibration. In this paper, we establish the optimal reverse conversion, showing that every [MATH]-zCDP mechanism satisfies [MATH]-GDP, where [MATH] and [MATH] uniquely solves the equation [MATH]. We also obtain simplified bounds [MATH], with sharp constants, which imply equivalence of the two frameworks up to constants. This explains why their minimax risks agree up to a constant rescaling of the privacy budget. We show that the squared conversion is strictly convex, which implies that converting zCDP to GDP before applying composition or group privacy yields a tighter GDP guarantee than converting afterward. We also derive the sharp conversion from bounded-range and logistic DP mechanisms (e.g., exponential mechanism) to GDP, where converting before composition but after group privacy gives the tighter guarantee.
