tldr: The paper tests whether machine learning on EMBER2024 features and raw bytes can predict the first-seen date of Windows executables or flag unreliable PE/COFF compile timestamps, finding regression fails but classification within tolerances partially works.
motivation: Temporal malware evaluation splits require reliable first-seen dates, yet such metadata comes from external services not equally available to all researchers, motivating an attempt to infer or validate timestamps from the executables themselves.
method: Using the EMBER2024 dataset, the authors train feature-based and raw-byte models under classification, regression, ranking, and latent-reliability formulations to estimate first-seen dates and to detect implausible compilation timestamps.
result: Direct first-seen regression errors span a large fraction of the collection window and no score yields useful chronological ordering, whereas classifiers can identify timestamps within specified tolerances of first seen and detect clearly implausible timestamps with high discrimination; substantial timestamp disagreement appears among both benign and malicious files.
conclusion: Current models cannot replace externally sourced first-seen metadata, but timestamp-reliability classification is feasible, establishing baselines and flagging timestamp reliability as a distinct direction for security-ML research.

title: What Must Be Done Here? Using A Bounded Application-Security Ontology At The Point Of Change
authors: Pedro Farinha
abstract: ArXiv:2611.01127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The security guidance that bears on code is real but scattered. It lives across secure-development frameworks, verification standards, controls catalogues, threat taxonomies, and, increasingly, normative regimes such as the EU's NIS2 -- and most of it is written for readers other than the engineer, or the AI assistant, at a point of change. Existing cybersecurity ontologies largely model attacks, indicators, and risk for detection and analysis, not the engineering-practice substance one must act on. This paper presents a use case for an existing bounded application-security ontology, AppSec Core, whose construction and validation are reported separately. We show how it is used. It makes the engineering-actionable fraction of those authorities addressable as a typed working set: the control objectives that apply, the practices that realize them, the mechanisms that implement them, and the evidence artifacts they expect, each traceable to the sources that justify it. We reach that working set from two entry points that recur in practice. Forward, from a code change: a change to authentication middleware scopes to its governing domain slice and returns the obligations the change must satisfy. Inverse, from a normative obligation: "make this NIS2-compliant" resolves a generic legal duty into the concrete engineering obligations it implies across slices, surfacing precisely the fraction of a mostly-governance regulation that lands in code. The same working set is what a human engineer reads and what an LLM-grounded assistant is handed as grounding. The use turns "read every applicable authority" into "satisfy this typed working set", for a code change or a compliance duty alike. The contribution is the demonstrated use; the artefact, its validation, and its governance are companion work.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a use case for a bounded application-security ontology (AppSec Core) that converts security guidance and normative regimes such as NIS2 into a typed, traceable working set of engineering obligations at the point of code change.
motivation: Security guidance bearing on code is scattered across frameworks, standards, and regulations, and is written for audiences other than the engineer or AI assistant making a change; existing cybersecurity ontologies model attacks and risk rather than engineering-practice substance.
method: A use-case demonstration of the existing AppSec Core ontology, entering either forward from a code change (e.g., authentication middleware) or inversely from a normative obligation (e.g., NIS2 compliance), resolving each into typed control objectives, practices, mechanisms, and evidence artifacts traceable to their sources.
result: The approach yields a single typed working set usable both by human engineers and as grounding for LLM-based assistants, reframing 'read every applicable authority' as 'satisfy this typed working set'.
conclusion: The contribution is the demonstrated use of the ontology; the artifact, its validation, and governance are reported in companion work, making this a software/cybersecurity engineering paper with no quantum information content.

title: A Large-Scale Evaluation Of Cookie Notice Privacy And Accessibility For Blind And Low Vision Users
authors: Maryam Mehrnezhad James M. Clarke
abstract: ArXiv:2611.01211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first large-scale privacy and accessibility evaluation of cookie notices across 2,061 domains for blind and low vision (BLV) users. Using a Playwright-based crawler, a custom NVDA screen reader add-on, and the Lighthouse and WAVE accessibility tools, we measure UK GDPR/PECR compliance, tracker activity across pre-interaction, post-accept, and post-reject phases, and cookie notice accessibility for screen reader users. We find that 51 % of sites display a cookie notice, of which (at least) 50 % violate UK GDPR/PECR requirements. Accepting a notice produces a mean five-fold increase in tracker activity, and degrades page landmark structure on one in five sites. While 95 % of notices are readable by a screen reader, only 37 % carry a meaningful title, 39 % are announced immediately on page load, and 42 % use descriptive button labels. We reveal a systemic correlation: cookie notices failing legal privacy requirements disproportionately exhibit the weakest screen reader accessibility. This compounding privacy burden on BLV users demands urgent intervention from developers, regulators, and standards bodies.
tldr: A large-scale measurement study of cookie notices across 2,061 domains finds widespread UK GDPR/PECR violations and poor screen-reader accessibility, with the weakest legal compliance correlating with the poorest accessibility for blind and low-vision users.
motivation: Cookie consent banners are pervasive, yet little is known about whether they comply with privacy law or are usable by blind and low-vision (BLV) users who rely on screen readers; the authors aim to quantify this compounding burden at scale.
method: The authors combine a Playwright-based crawler, a custom NVDA screen reader add-on, and the Lighthouse and WAVE accessibility tools to measure legal compliance, tracker activity in pre-interaction, post-accept, and post-reject phases, and screen-reader accessibility of notices.
result: 51% of sites show a cookie notice, of which at least 50% violate UK GDPR/PECR; accepting a notice produces a mean five-fold rise in tracker activity and degrades landmark structure on one in five sites, while only 37% of notices have meaningful titles and 42% use descriptive button labels.
conclusion: Cookie notices impose a disproportionate, systemic privacy and accessibility burden on BLV users, motivating intervention from developers, regulators, and standards bodies.

title: Letter To A Young Black Mathematician: History, Storytelling, And Belonging In Mathematics
authors: Ranthony A. Clark
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What does it mean to tell the story of a mathematician? Written as a letter to a young Black mathematician, this article reflects on how stories shape our understanding of mathematics and our sense of belonging within the mathematical community. Through the lens of Hidden Figures Revealed, a project documenting Black mathematicians at The Ohio State University, I discuss humanity, mathematics, and context as three guiding principles for mathematical storytelling. In particular, I reflect on how this framework emerged through archival research, shaped historical narratives, and informed mathematical learning experiences.
tldr: A reflective letter on storytelling, history, and belonging in mathematics, focused on Black mathematicians and the Hidden Figures Revealed project.
motivation: The article aims to explore how narratives shape mathematical identity and community belonging, especially for young Black mathematicians.
method: It uses archival research and personal reflection from the Hidden Figures Revealed project documenting Black mathematicians at Ohio State University.
result: The author proposes humanity, mathematics, and context as guiding principles for mathematical storytelling and discusses how this framework informed historical narratives and learning experiences.
conclusion: The paper argues that storytelling is central to understanding mathematics as a human endeavor and to fostering belonging in the mathematical community.

title: Order Continuity Of Induced Homomorphisms Between Free Banach Lattices
authors: Pedro Tradacete Ra\'ul E. Pariente-Mart\'in
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a bounded operator between Banach spaces and let [MATH] be the lattice homomorphism induced by [MATH] between the corresponding free [MATH]-convex Banach lattices generated by [MATH] and [MATH]. We show that [MATH] is order continuous if and only if it is either zero or a lattice isomorphic embedding. For [MATH], this holds precisely when [MATH] is zero or an isomorphic embedding, while for [MATH], apart from the zero operator, [MATH] must be an embedding and the pair [MATH] must have the operator-extension property POE-[MATH]. In addition, we study when [MATH] is order dense or majorizing in [MATH] for [MATH].
tldr: The paper characterizes order continuity of lattice homomorphisms induced by bounded operators between free p-convex Banach lattices.
motivation: The authors study when the natural lattice homomorphism induced by an operator between Banach spaces preserves order-continuity properties in the associated free Banach lattices.
method: They analyze bounded operators and their induced lattice homomorphisms, proving equivalences with zero maps or lattice isomorphic embeddings, with special cases for p=1 and p=∞ involving the operator-extension property POE.
result: The main theorem shows order continuity holds iff the induced homomorphism is zero or a lattice isomorphic embedding, with additional operator-extension conditions in the p=∞ case; order density and majorization are also examined.
conclusion: These results provide structural criteria for order continuity in free Banach lattices, but the work is purely functional-analytic and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Comparison Of Parallel Iterative Methods For Ilu Triangular Solves
authors: C. C. Pain S. Dargaville
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact triangular solves parallelise poorly, limited by the size and number of the level sets, so on GPUs the factors from incomplete LU (ILU) factorisations are often solved approximately with parallel iterative methods. We compare four such methods: a Jacobi method, an Incomplete Sparse Approximate Inverse (ISAI), GMRES polynomials, and AIRG, a reduction multigrid built on GMRES polynomials, for which we introduce a parallel coarse/fine splitting that bounds the diagonal dominance ratio of the fine-fine block. We test them with ILU(0) and ILU(1) factors of canonical PDE problems and 91 SuiteSparse/Matrix Market matrices, the latter on a single GPU. AIRG is the most robust on the PDE factors, with nearly flat iteration counts under refinement and no per-problem tuning, but has the largest setup and memory costs. GMRES polynomials are more robust than the Jacobi method at a similar cost. As the inner solve of an ILU preconditioner with tuned inner iteration counts, ISAI gives the largest median speedups over a hipSPARSE exact triangular solve (4.5[MATH] and 6.8[MATH] for ILU(0) and ILU(1)), though this was dominated by smaller problems; on the largest ILU(1) problems all four methods give similar median speedups of 2.1-2.6[MATH].
tldr: The paper compares parallel iterative methods for approximate ILU triangular solves on GPUs, focusing on numerical linear algebra performance rather than quantum information.
motivation: Exact triangular solves parallelize poorly, so ILU-preconditioned solvers often use approximate parallel iterative triangular solves on GPUs.
method: The authors compare Jacobi, ISAI, GMRES polynomials, and AIRG on ILU(0)/ILU(1) factors from PDE problems and SuiteSparse matrices, including a new parallel coarse/fine splitting for AIRG.
result: AIRG is most robust on PDE factors with nearly flat iteration counts, ISAI yields the largest median speedups with tuned inner iterations, and all methods perform similarly on the largest ILU(1) problems.
conclusion: The study provides practical guidance on trade-offs among robustness, setup/memory cost, and speedup for parallel approximate ILU triangular solves on GPUs.

title: A Parallel Adaptive Proximal Admm For Linearly Constrained Separable Composite Optimization Problems
authors: Leandro F. Maia, Renato D. C. Monteiro, Gilson N. Silva
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose and analyze an adaptive proximal alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), based on Jacobi-type updates, for linearly constrained separable nonconvex composite optimization problems. The objective consists of two block-separable functions, one continuously differentiable and weakly convex, and the other convex and Lipschitz continuous. The proposed method is adaptive to all problem parameters and allows inexact solutions of the block proximal subproblems. At each iteration, we solve all block subproblems in parallel, then apply a novel test to decide whether to update the Lagrange multiplier and/or the penalty parameter. Without any rank assumptions on the constraint matrices, we establish an [MATH] iteration-complexity bound for obtaining an approximate first-order stationary point. This matches the best-known complexity for cyclic proximal ADMM methods and improves the existing complexity of Jacobi-type schemes in this general nonconvex setting. Numerical experiments on a nonconvex quadratic program illustrate the proposed method's computational benefits.
tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive Jacobi-type proximal ADMM for linearly constrained separable nonconvex composite optimization with inexact subproblem solves and an O(1/epsilon^2)-style iteration-complexity guarantee.
motivation: Cyclic proximal ADMM has well-understood complexity in nonconvex settings, but parallel (Jacobi-type) variants lack equally strong guarantees and typically require tuning of penalty parameters.
method: Two block-separable objectives (one weakly convex and smooth, one convex and Lipschitz) are minimized in parallel per iteration, with a novel test deciding whether to update the Lagrange multiplier and/or penalty parameter; all parameters are adapted automatically and subproblems may be solved inexactly.
result: Without rank assumptions on the constraint matrices, an iteration-complexity bound for approximate first-order stationarity is established, matching the best known cyclic-ADMM complexity and improving on existing Jacobi-type schemes; numerical experiments on a nonconvex quadratic program show computational benefits.
conclusion: The adaptive parallel proximal ADMM is a practical and theoretically sound method for nonconvex separable composite optimization, though it lies outside quantum information research.

title: Threat Modeling Intimate Partner Abuse In Agentic Systems
authors: Natalie Grace Brigham, Eugene Bagdasarian, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic systems are AI-powered technologies capable of autonomous action within digital environments, such as sending emails or making reservations. They are deeply connected to external tools as well as users' data and resources, making them vulnerable to attacks which exploit their access and capabilities. In this work, we apply the technology-facilitated abuse threat model, in the context of intimate partner violence and surveillance, to these systems, revealing threats that require deliberate investigation and mitigation. We categorize attacks based on system ownership: (1) Abuser-as-owner attacks demonstrate how agentic systems make existing forms of technology-facilitated abuse far easier and more scalable. (2) Victim-survivor-as-owner attacks show how agentic systems create a new attack surface which abusers can exploit. In light of these risks, we outline research and development directions for effective mitigation strategies.
tldr: This paper applies a technology-facilitated abuse threat model from intimate partner violence to AI agentic systems, cataloging attacks based on system ownership.
motivation: Agentic AI systems have deep access to tools, user data, and resources, creating attack surfaces that could intensify surveillance and abuse in intimate partner violence contexts, a risk the authors argue needs deliberate investigation.
method: The authors adapt an existing technology-facilitated abuse threat modeling framework to agentic systems, organizing threats into two categories: abuser-as-owner and victim-survivor-as-owner attacks.
result: The analysis shows that agentic systems both scale up existing forms of technology-facilitated abuse and introduce a new attack surface exploitable by abusers when the victim-survivor owns the system.
conclusion: The authors outline research and development directions for mitigation strategies to address these security and safety risks in agentic AI.

title: VeilFL: Two-Stage Accountability For Anonymous Federated Learning
authors: Varesh Mishra, Aysajan Abidin, Bart Preneel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.01082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.
tldr: VeilFL is a two-aggregator anonymous federated learning protocol that adds staged accountability and controlled identity opening to PINE using anonymous credentials and threshold committees.
motivation: Anonymous credentials in federated learning hide client participation but also make repeated misconduct hard to link, creating a need for accountability without persistent identifiers.
method: The protocol binds submissions to a hidden credential secret, detects duplicate submissions per round, and uses two threshold committees for staged tracing and identity recovery after logged faults.
result: The prototype shows submission creation at 2.11 ms median, verification at 3.01 ms, batch verification at 1.86 ms per submission for 1,000 submissions, and each opening stage within 4.3 ms.
conclusion: VeilFL provides duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, and controlled two-stage opening while preserving PINE's privacy and validity guarantees under stated assumptions.

title: Pop Goes The Verifier: Phoneme-Targeted Data Poisoning Of Voice Liveness Detection
authors: Amith Kamath Belman Eshaq Jamdar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.01095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many Automated Speaker Verification Systems (ASVs) commonly employ liveliness detection techniques, such as VoicePop, which identify genuine speech by analyzing low- frequency pop bursts from plosive phonemes using Gammatone Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (GFCC) and an SVM classifier. While effective against traditional replay attacks, such systems are vulnerable to data poisoning techniques. Prior work shows that broadly applied SyntheticPop attacks can collapse model to accuracy to as low as 14.01% using only 20% poisoned samples, but the resulting artifacts are easily detectable when visualizing the waveform energies. This paper introduces Pop Goes the Verifier, a stealthier phoneme injection poisoning attack. By leveraging FastSpeech 2 (FS2) with a modified HiFi-GAN vocoder, we inject localized pop bursts at plosive phoneme locations and overlay subtle Gaussian noise to reduce the visibility of injected artifacts in waveform and spectrogram analysis. Using the ASVSpoof 2019 as the dataset, we observe that the approach achieves a moderate poisoning attack while providing greater resistance to signal-level inspection than the original SyntheticPop attack.
tldr: The paper presents a phoneme-targeted data poisoning attack against VoicePop-style voice liveness detection using FastSpeech 2 and a modified HiFi-GAN vocoder.
motivation: Voice liveness detection systems such as VoicePop are effective against replay attacks but vulnerable to data poisoning; prior SyntheticPop attacks leave detectable waveform artifacts.
method: The authors inject localized pop bursts at plosive phoneme locations using FastSpeech 2 with a modified HiFi-GAN vocoder and overlay subtle Gaussian noise to make poisoning artifacts less visible in waveform and spectrogram analysis.
result: On ASVSpoof 2019, the attack achieves moderate poisoning effectiveness while resisting signal-level inspection better than the original SyntheticPop attack.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a stealthier poisoning strategy against voice liveness detection, though it remains outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: When Are Dividend Barriers Optimal? A Distributional Characterization In Renewal Risk Models
authors: Linyu Miao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.00827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the finite-horizon optimal dividend problem in a renewal risk model with unrestricted dividend payments, examining how claim-size distributions determine barrier optimality. Under general assumptions on a fixed interclaim-time distribution, we prove that exponential claims admit a globally optimal barrier for every positive safety loading, positive discount rate and finite horizon. Conversely, within the class of claim-size distributions with continuous nondecreasing hazard, every nonexponential law admits one fixed premium--discount pair for which no barrier is globally optimal at any sufficiently long horizon. These results establish, within this distribution class, an equivalence between exponentially distributed claims and the existence of a globally optimal barrier for every parameter combination in the stated range. Numerical examples compare exponential and Gamma claims with the same mean and illustrate how the claim-size distribution changes the structure of dividend decisions.
tldr: The paper characterizes when barrier dividend strategies are optimal in renewal risk models depending on the claim-size distribution.
motivation: Optimal dividend problems in risk theory seek dividend strategies that maximize expected discounted payouts, and barrier strategies are common but not universally optimal.
method: The authors analyze finite-horizon optimal dividend problems under a fixed interclaim-time distribution and general claim-size distributions, proving equivalence results within a continuous nondecreasing hazard class.
result: Exponential claims admit a globally optimal barrier for all positive safety loading, discount rate, and finite horizon, while every nonexponential law in the class has some parameter pair where no barrier is globally optimal at long horizons.
conclusion: Within the studied distribution class, barrier optimality for all parameter combinations is equivalent to exponential claim sizes, illustrating how claim distributions shape dividend strategy structure.
